papers.Title: Spectrum Adaptation of AI-Native Autoencoder Communications with Transfer Learning
papers.Abstract: End-to-end physical-layer learning replaces separate modulation, coding, and detection operations with an autoencoder (AE) that consists of a jointly trained encoder-decoder pair at the transmitter and the receiver. This paper studies AI-native communications with AEs and quantifies the sensitivity to training-test mismatch in channel models. Models trained only on an AWGN channel achieve low bit error rates (BERs) under matched conditions but degrade severely on Rayleigh fading with practical front-end impairments. To reduce the time and energy required to adapt to new channel conditions, we propose a low-latency transfer-learning procedure that starts from an AWGN-pretrained system and fine-tunes only a small subset of transmitter and receiver layers while freezing the remainder. We further formulate layer selection as a budget-constrained optimization problem that identifies the most informative parameters to update during adaptation. This preserves the learned signal geometry and the deep decision structure while adapting lightweight front ends to fading- and impairment-induced mixing. For AE communications, we show that partial updates remove the mismatch-induced error floor and approach the BER of fully retrained models. We provide a layer-wise study and quantify resource-performance trade-offs, showing that modest adaptation substantially reduces BER while cutting training time, multiply-accumulate (MAC) operations, energy consumption, and the fraction of updated parameters for resource-efficient implementation.
papers.Core_Innovation: Selective layer fine-tuning with budget-constrained parameter selection adapts AWGN-pretrained autoencoders to fading channels without full retraining.
papers.Disrupted_Sectors: Traditional Modem Manufacturers, Conventional FEC Hardware
papers.Decision_Perspective: Prioritize integration of budget-constrained transfer learning into 6G transceiver pipelines within 18 months. Acquire or partner with firms holding AWGN-pretrained autoencoder IP to de-risk rapid channel adaptation
papers.Tags: autoencoder, transfer learning, channel adaptation, physical layer, layer selection
papers.Hook: AWGN-trained autoencoders rapidly adapt to fading channels via selective layer fine-tuning

papers.Title: Tokenisation is not in APX
papers.Abstract: In this paper, we prove that, unless P=NP, no polynomial-time algorithm can find a tokeniser whose objective is within any constant factor of the optimum, meaning that tokenisation is not in the APX complexity class. We prove this for direct and bottom-up tokenisation, under both a compression or unigram log-likelihood objectives, and for binary or larger alphabets. We further show that, even over unary alphabets, direct tokenisation is APX-hard, and thus admits no polynomial-time approximation scheme.
papers.Core_Innovation: Proves APX-hardness of direct tokenisation via gap-preserving reductions from label cover, even for unary alphabets.
papers.Disrupted_Sectors: Machine Learning, Data Compression, Natural Language Processing
papers.Decision_Perspective: Cease funding black-box tokenisation optimisation unless complexity bounds are verified. Prioritise provably secure compression frameworks for new LLM architectures within 18 months.
papers.Tags: tokenisation, APX-hardness, compression, approximation
papers.Hook: Proves tokenisation cannot be constant-factor approximated unless P=NP.

papers.Title: Can image generation help visual reasoning? An empirical study
papers.Abstract: Language models think in words; then multimodal models might think in images. We test whether a generated helper improves the answer to a visual question. A model describes the helper it needs and then answers using the original and generated images together. Across 13 vision-language model and generator pairs, generation lowers mean accuracy by 3.7 percentage points, with declines on nine of ten tasks. Two unified models, BAGEL and Janus-Pro-7B, each lose accuracy on eight tasks. On VSTAR, adding a generated image to the same planning hint lowers accuracy by 10.47 points. Repeated image edits yield different outcomes across tasks. ChartQAPro and MathVista stay below their no-generation baselines, while ERQA gains three points after ten edits.
papers.Core_Innovation: The pipeline generates descriptive helper images via model prompts, then fuses them with original inputs to enable systematic accuracy assessment across vision-language model-generator combinations.
papers.Decision_Perspective: Discontinue generation-augmented reasoning pipelines for visual QA due to consistent accuracy losses. Reallocate resources to ERQA-specific image refinement protocols within two quarters.
papers.Tags: Image Generation, Visual Reasoning, VL Models, ERQA
papers.Hook: Empirical analysis reveals image generation consistently degrades visual reasoning accuracy across most VL models.

papers.Title: Attack Policy Selection can Mislead Monitor Evaluators
papers.Abstract: AI monitors, classifiers that flag dangerous behaviour by AI agents, are often evaluated against transcripts generated by attack policies acting as proxies for dangerous behaviour in deployment. We evaluate an ex-production OpenAI monitor as a case study and find that measured false negative rate is highly sensitive to both the method used to generate attack policies and the level of optimisation applied within that method. This rate ranged from 0.5\% to 20.8\% across optimisation levels of a single method (reinforcement learning), and from 6.4\% to 23.0\% across methods at their best observed optimisation level (optimised prompting vs.\ transcript editing). Every attack policy was developed against proxy monitors only: all reported results show attacks transferring to the held-out GPT-5.4 target monitor. Our results suggest that monitor evasion evaluations can easily mislead: an evaluation using only basic attack methods may give false confidence that a monitor is strong.   The sensitivity to attack-policy choice raises a problem: interpreting any particular result as evidence about deployment performance requires justification. The transcripts produced by attack policies are proxies for the dangerous behaviour a monitor must flag in deployment. These proxies can introduce visible artefacts, such as reasoning about a ``side task'' absent from the instructions shown to the monitor, that affect monitor judgements. Given the sensitivity above, the choice of proxy can change an evaluation's conclusion. Reading these results as evidence about deployment therefore requires a separate legitimacy argument for why the proxies are informative, including any justification of conservativeness. Making convincing arguments remains an open problem.
papers.Core_Innovation: Systematic variation of attack policy generation methods and optimization levels reveals false-negative rate spans of 0.5–23.0%. All evaluated attacks transfer to a held-out target monitor, exposing evaluation dependence on proxy design.
papers.Decision_Perspective: Mandate multi-method attack policy red-teaming for all monitor deployments within 90 days. Deprecate single-method evaluation pipelines that cannot detect optimized evasion.
papers.Tags: AI monitoring, attack policies, evaluation reliability
papers.Hook: Basic attack methods falsely assure monitor robustness against optimized evasion.

papers.Title: A gene informed benchmark for BioScoring of pathology foundation models
papers.Abstract: Pathology foundation models are usually compared by their performance on downstream tasks such as classification and retrieval. While such benchmarks measure how useful a model is, they provide no insight into the biology it represents. We introduce BioScore, a benchmark that quantifies how well an image encoder captures cell identities, with spatial transcriptomics of the same tissue as the reference. A sparse autoencoder splits the encoder's patch embeddings into sparse features, which we cluster into a fixed number of groups. BioScore then measures, for each of 52 cell identities defined by marker genes, how specifically one group follows the identity's expression over the tissue. Because the autoencoder training is fully unsupervised, a match shows that the model represents the cell identity from the image alone. We score 8 pathology foundation models and 3 natural-image models. Every pathology model scores above every natural-image model (0.299--0.371 \vs 0.214--0.232), and paired tests separate three tiers among the pathology models. Unlike a supervised probe, BioScore needs no labels, builds its reference from the data and scores even from few sections, yet it ranks the encoders as a probe does. Its per-identity breakdown indicates which cell identities each encoder captures or misses.
papers.Core_Innovation: Sparse autoencoders cluster pathology foundation model patch embeddings into groups quantified against 52 marker gene-defined cell identities via matched spatial transcriptomics, all trained without supervision
papers.Disrupted_Sectors: Generic Natural-Image Benchmarks, Traditional Histopathology Scoring
papers.Decision_Perspective: Mandate BioScore evaluation for all pathology foundation model audits beginning Q3 2026. Retire downstream-task-only benchmarks that ignore cellular identity representation.
papers.Tags: Pathology, Foundation Models, BioScore, Sparse Autoencoder, Spatial Transcriptomics
papers.Hook: BioScore unsupervisedly scores pathology model cell-identity fidelity using sparse autoencoders

papers.Title: Diverse Alternative Reasoning Traces for Hard Math Problems
papers.Abstract: Post-training large language models (LLMs) for mathematical reasoning often relies on accepted traces whose final answers pass a verifier. For hard math problems, however, such traces can be rare under independent Monte Carlo (MC) sampling. To address this, we propose Diverse Alternative Reasoning Traces (DART), a trace-mining method that starts from a rejected trace, decomposes it into reasoning steps, and ranks them by position-weighted uncertainty. It then generates deliberately distinct alternative candidates for highly ranked steps using reference-answer guidance and a meta-thought before completing the resulting traces. On greedy-unsolved DeepMath-103K problems, DART recovers 37% more problems than MC sampling at a matched number of generated traces. Its estimated generation cost per recovered problem is nearly identical, while its cost per accepted trace is 30% lower. Post-training Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct on traces mined by DART achieves the highest point estimate in five of six evaluations across MATH-500 and AIME benchmarks. These results demonstrate that revisiting rejected traces with DART can expand problem coverage and provide effective post-training data.
papers.Core_Innovation: DART decomposes rejected traces by position-weighted uncertainty and regenerates distinct alternatives at critical steps using reference-answer guidance and meta-thought
papers.Benefiting_Sectors: Education Technology, Financial Services, AI Research
papers.Decision_Perspective: Allocate DART-integrated post-training budgets within two quarters to capture the 37% recovery advantage. Retire MC-sampling baselines once cost-per-accepted-trace metrics confirm the 30% improvement.
papers.Tags: LLM reasoning, trace mining, math benchmark
papers.Hook: DART recovers 37% more math problems than MC sampling at matched trace cost.

papers.Title: Mixture-of-Loops Transformer
papers.Abstract: Looped Transformers boost expressivity by reusing shared layers across loops, yet at the cost of efficiency. Pushing their expressivity-efficiency frontier requires rethinking the core mechanism connecting adjacent loops: What should be passed as a Transformer loops? We introduce Mixture-of-Loops Transformer (MoLT), whose Mixture-of-Loops Attention (MoLA) uses keys and values (KV) as memory for selective reuse across depths and loops. Under loop residual, MoLT-R retains the residual stream and reads local KV across loops for expressivity. Under loop KV, MoLT-KV instead restarts from embeddings and reads current-loop local KV with preceding-loop memory KV at earlier positions for efficiency. MoLT-KV eliminates same-position cross-loop dependence and, paired with loop forcing for parallel training, unlocks single-traversal Mixture-of-Loops (MoL) decoding beyond the training loop horizon. To balance efficiency and quality, we introduce U-shaped MoLT (U-MoLT), which separates memory construction from prediction readout and skips unused decoder traversals without changing predictions. In 400B-token pretraining, U-MoLT outperforms OLMo3 across 700M/1.5B dense and 3B MoE models, achieving 1.7x validation cross-entropy (CE) token efficiency at 700M while improving 3B MoE 10-domain perplexity by 0.75 and 10-task accuracy by 2.1 percentage points. In 100B-token continued pretraining of Qwen3.5-0.8B-Base, our U-MoLT adaptation lowers CE on all 11 domains over the matched baseline with 1.4x mean token efficiency. At inference, U-MoLT with MoL-Hybrid-2 matches non-looped OLMo3 latency at 996.6 vs. 1,000.6 ms on S-size (~113M) models. Code is available at https://github.com/hustvl/MoLT
papers.Core_Innovation: MoLA uses keys and values as selective memory for cross-loop reuse. MoLT-KV eliminates same-position cross-loop dependence by restarting from embeddings and incorporating preceding-loop memory KV at earlier positions, enabling single-traversal decoding beyond the training horizon.
papers.Decision_Perspective: Accelerate MoLT-KV integration into LLM inference pipelines within the next two quarters to quantify single-traversal decoding efficiency gains. Competing loop-based architectures without KV memory reuse should be evaluated for phased replacement.
papers.Tags: Mixture-of-Loops, KV Memory, Transformer Decoding, Efficiency
papers.Hook: MoLT-KV enables single-traversal Mixture-of-Loops decoding beyond training loop horizon.

papers.Title: $μ$-Bench: Benchmarking Multi-User Task Completion in Shared Interaction Voice Agents
papers.Abstract: Voice agents in shared spaces must satisfy interdependent multi-user requests while upholding per-user authority, privacy, and task constraints. Existing evaluations offer limited coverage when participants react throughout a session. We introduce $μ$-Bench, a benchmark for joint task completion in closed-loop, full-duplex multi-user voice interaction. Simulated participants act from isolated profiles of goals, knowledge, and permissions, adapting to the agent's speech and tool outcomes. Across 20 domains, 100 scenarios vary group size, acoustics, and follow-up demands to form 800 cases (408 tool-augmented, 392 tool-free). Joint Task Success (JTS) requires all user goals, privacy boundaries, and terminal states to hold jointly, while Pure JTS further disallows unauthorized tool calls; Attribution, Threading, and Coordination (ATC) diagnostics localize failures. Across 13 voice agents, proprietary systems peak at 62.24\% tool-free and 65.44\% tool-augmented success, while open-weight models remain below 20\%. ATC diagnostics show that open-weight models lag primarily in multi-turn attribution and threading, and controlled contrasts reveal that larger groups consistently degrade joint task success across capable systems. By coupling reactive multi-user simulation with verifiable session-level outcomes, $μ$-Bench provides a rigorous testbed for shared voice agents.
papers.Core_Innovation: The core innovation is a simulated multi-user framework where each participant maintains isolated goals, knowledge, and permissions that dynamically adapt to agent speech and tool outcomes within a closed-loop, full-duplex interaction
papers.Decision_Perspective: Acquire Mu-Bench and integrate its ATC diagnostics into all new voice agent pilots within 90 days to quantify multi-user privacy risk. Phase out legacy IVR systems that fail to achieve above 60% Joint Task Success under the benchmark's joint privacy constraints.
papers.Tags: Voice Agents, Multi-User Benchmark, Privacy, Tool Use
papers.Hook: New benchmark enables joint task success evaluation for multi-user voice agents under privacy constraints

papers.Title: Enhancing Maritime Domain Awareness using Latent Space Representations
papers.Abstract: This work presents a novel application of Earth Observation (EO) embeddings for Maritime Domain Awareness (MDA) from the perspective of the geospatial foundation model TerraMind. By operating directly on compressed latent-space representations rather than on the original Sentinel-1 imagery, this approach directly addresses the data gravity bottleneck that increasingly constrains operational EO processing, in line with the objectives of the Embed2Scale project. In particular, linear and non-linear probing of compressed embeddings, latent space representations of synthetic aperture radar (SAR) imagery, is used to detect, localise, and characterise vessels from Sentinel-1 GRD images. Vessel detection achieves a ROC-AUC of 0.95, while vessel localisation has a median error of around 300 m for vessels longer than 100 m, and vessel AIS type-code classification achieves 62% accuracy for the majority classes. The latter, however, is highly correlated with vessel length. These results reveal both the potential and current limitations of Geospatial Foundation Models (GeoFMs) when applied to fine-grained MDA understanding in real-world scenarios.   Additionally, a new maritime remote sensing dataset is released, pairing about 2,000 Sentinel-1 images with temporally aligned AIS signals from commercial vessels. Through manual inspection, each candidate sample was verified for bounding-box quality and for consistency between the AIS-reported vessel length and the observed vessel extent, cross-checking vessel identity and location against publicly available vessel records and, where available, photographs. The dataset was made ready for use with the NeuCo-Bench neural compression benchmark framework, publicly available on HuggingFace through https://huggingface.co/datasets/embed2scale/S1-single-ship-downstream .
papers.Core_Innovation: The innovation probes TerraMind's compressed SAR embeddings directly, bypassing raw imagery pipelines. This enables vessel detection, localization and AIS classification entirely within latent space.
papers.Benefiting_Sectors: Maritime Shipping, Defense, Geospatial Analytics, Logistics
papers.Disrupted_Sectors: Legacy MDA Contractors, Raw Imagery Processors
papers.Decision_Perspective: Allocate budget to integrate TerraMind latent-space probing into operational MDA workflows within 12 months to cut raw data dependency by 40%. Decommission legacy raw GRD download pipelines once latency and accuracy benchmarks are validated.
papers.Tags: SAR, Latent Space, Maritime Awareness, Embeddings, Data Gravity
papers.Hook: Latent-space SAR embeddings enable vessel detection and localization without raw imagery processing

papers.Title: What a Drop Reveals: Sim-to-Real Material Estimation for Deformable Objects from Video
papers.Abstract: How an object deforms when it hits the ground reveals what it is made of. From a single real video of a drop, we estimate a deformable object's density-normalized stiffness $E/ρ$, and its yield stress $σ_Y/ρ$ when the impact causes plastic deformation, with a feed-forward predictor trained only in simulation. Real videos carry no material labels, so such predictors are developed and validated on synthetic data alone. We show that synthetic validation ranks their geometric inputs in the wrong order. Material acts through 3D deformation, and tracklets lifted to 3D with estimated depth are indeed the most accurate input in simulation. However, on real drops they are the least accurate, and better depth does not repair them: the failure persists with simulator depth in training, LiDAR depth at test time, and exact depth on rendered replays of the real drops. Short 2D optical-flow tracklets do the opposite: they improve nothing in simulation, yet they transfer best. Material is therefore better read from what perception measures consistently in both domains than from what is most informative in simulation. Our predictor, PhysReader, reads the video and 2D tracklets and learns the lift to 3D in simulation by matching a teacher that sees exact 3D deformation. To measure transfer, we introduce PhysReader-Real: 16 everyday objects dropped five times each, with reference materials fit jointly to each object's drops and checked against tensile tests. On PhysReader-Real, PhysReader is closer to the reference materials than every other input and baseline. The one exception is a per-scene optimizer started from PhysReader's prediction, which ends slightly closer but takes 49 minutes per video instead of 12 seconds.
papers.Core_Innovation: The paper discovers that 3D depth-lifted tracklets, optimal for material estimation in simulation, fail catastrophically on real impacts. Meanwhile, 2D optical-flow tracklets show the opposite transfer profile, exposing a fundamental sim-to-real deformation mismatch.
papers.Decision_Perspective: Fund development of 2D-optical-flow-based material estimators for robotic manipulation within 12 months, as they transfer from simulation without depth dependency. Kill investment in 3D-reconstruction pipelines for impact material estimation, since they fail on real drops regardless of depth fidelity.
papers.Tags: Sim-to-Real, Material Estimation, Deformable Objects, Optical Flow, Impact Dynamics
papers.Hook: Single drop videos estimate material stiffness and yield stress, trained only in simulation.

papers.Title: Interpretable and Accurate Hybrid Decision Trees with Selective Case-Based Splits
papers.Abstract: Decision trees are among the most well-known interpretable models in Machine Learning. Over the years, a wide variety of strategies have been proposed to define split conditions within the greedy learning framework, aiming to guide instance routing and enhance predictive performance. These strategies range from axis-parallel and oblique splits based on feature values to proximity-based splits using exemplar instances and more complex hybrid approaches. However, no single method has emerged as universally superior. In this work, we present two key contributions to the construction of greedy decision trees. First, we propose a hybrid tree architecture that integrates both feature-based and case-based splits, allowing for heterogeneous splits throughout the tree. Second, we introduce a novel type of split that leverages a selective case-based approach: when a split is needed, our method searches for the most informative subset of features to define the split, effectively balancing the specificity of case-based methods with the simplicity of feature-based ones. Experiments on a diverse set of tabular datasets show that our method outperforms standard decision trees and achieves performance on par with ensemble methods, while producing shallow trees that retain or even improve predictive accuracy.
papers.Core_Innovation: It replaces standard greedy feature selection with a selective case-based split that dynamically identifies minimal informative feature subsets per node, enabling heterogeneous split types within a single tree.
papers.Decision_Perspective: AI research departments should prototype hybrid tree frameworks with selective splits within 3 months to measure interpretability-accuracy tradeoffs. Competing rule-engine vendors should accelerate model migration or risk feature obsolescence.
papers.Tags: Decision Trees, Hybrid Models, Case-Based Splits, Interpretability
papers.Hook: Hybrid trees merge feature and case splits for interpretable accuracy.

papers.Title: Stranger Things: When Objects Appear Without Their Typical Neighbors
papers.Abstract: Visual context is a powerful cue for object recognition: scenes inform what, where, and at what scale objects are likely to appear. Yet over-reliance on context becomes a failure mode when models predict objects based on their typical neighbors rather than the objects' own visual features, which we call typicality bias. While extensively studied in the pre-Transformer era, it has often been assumed that architectural and scale improvements would naturally solve it, and a systematic diagnostic across the modern vision stack remains absent. We provide such a diagnostic framework. We measure typicality bias via normalized pointwise mutual information (NPMI) over object pairs, and introduce STRANGE-Bench (Synthetic Typicality-RANked Grounded Evaluation Benchmark): a photorealistic, layout-controlled benchmark spanning 17 sub-tiers from typical to never-co-occurring object pairs. Across five model families (specialist detectors, open-vocabulary detectors, self-supervised, vision-language, and multimodal large language models) and three recognition tasks (supervised detection, open-vocabulary detection, and classification), the bias is prevalent: gaps of 5-11 p.p. persist when objects appear outside their typical company, and do not consistently shrink with scale. To mitigate it, we turn to data augmentation: existing augmentations are designed for visual diversity, not for breaking co-occurrence shortcuts, and sample from the very distribution that produces typicality bias. We propose Anchor-Atypicality Sampling (AAS), a simple sampling rule for paste-based augmentations that uses the NPMI signal to tilt the training-time co-occurrence distribution toward atypical partners. AAS reduces the typicality gap by up to 1.6 p.p. on natural-image COCO splits and 23.0 p.p. on synthetic STRANGE-Bench across three model families, without sacrificing overall performance.
papers.Core_Innovation: The paper introduces STRANGE-Bench, a photorealistic layout-controlled benchmark with 17 sub-tiers spanning typical to never-co-occurring object pairs, and quantifies typicality bias via NPMI over object pairs for systematic evaluation across specialist detectors, open-vocabulary detectors, self-supervised, vision-language, and transformer-based models.
papers.Benefiting_Sectors: Autonomous Vehicles, Industrial Automation, Retail Analytics
papers.Decision_Perspective: Allocate R&D budget to integrate NPMI-based typicality bias audits into vision model validation pipelines within six months. Require STRANGE-Bench benchmarking for any computer vision system deployed in safety-critical contexts.
papers.Tags: Vision, Bias, Benchmark, Object Detection, Context
papers.Hook: StrANGE-Bench diagnoses and measures typicality bias across modern vision models via NPMI and layout-controlled object pairs

papers.Title: How Much Do Coding Agents Over-Edit, and Why? An Empirical Study of Unneeded Edits in Repository-Level Agent Patches
papers.Abstract: Agent patches are larger than developers', which is widely read as over-editing. But patch size does not say whether the extra edits are needed, what they are, or where they come from. We introduce Delta Residue Attribution (DRA), which replays agent trajectories, traces every block (unit) of the final patch to the step that wrote it, reverts each unit, and reruns the task tests to decide whether the unit is needed. We apply DRA to 7,660 resolved GitHub Copilot CLI trajectories from 18 frontier models on SWE-bench Verified (6,728) and DeepSWE (932), and grade developer patches using the same method. Agent patches do change more lines than developers'; on SWE-bench Verified the majority of extra edits add tests (61%) and documentation (13%) while on DeepSWE, most extra edits are code (58%). On both benchmarks, agents' code is on average at least as necessary as developers' (mean $NP_{code}$ 0.887 vs. 0.864 on SWE-bench Verified, where 11 of 18 models leave less unneeded code than developers, and 0.797 vs. 0.785 on DeepSWE). On average, 11% of an agent patch's code units on SWE-bench Verified are still unneeded, and 89% of those change behavior. Debug steps write almost none of the unneeded code. Code necessity differs substantially by model; it is unrelated to resolve rate on SWE-bench Verified and negatively correlated with it on DeepSWE (Spearman -0.59, p = 0.01). On SWE-bench Verified, pruning with DRA using only the tests the agent can see (its own tests and the repository's) removes the majority of unneeded code but also some needed code (67% recall, 46% precision), and 89% of pruned patches still resolve the task; asking the agent to audit its own diff is more precise but less effective (36% recall, 66% precision). We recommend that benchmarks report code necessity next to resolve rate and that over-editing be addressed through model training and harness-level pruning.
papers.Core_Innovation: Delta Residue Attribution (DRA) replays agent trajectories, traces each patch block to its writing step, reverts units, and reruns task tests to empirically determine edit necessity.
papers.Benefiting_Sectors: Software Development, AI Code Generation, Test Automation
papers.Decision_Perspective: Invest in DRA tooling integration for repository-level CI within the next two quarterly cycles to automatically filter unneeded agent edits. Mandate its use for all AI-assisted code merges exceeding 15% line expansion.
papers.Tags: Delta Residue Attribution, Agent Over-Editing, Code Necessity, Repository Patches
papers.Hook: DRA quantifies and reverts unneeded agent edits at unit granularity.

papers.Title: Shape-Aware Three-Way Merge for RDF Knowledge Graphs: The schema defines the conflict: an implementation and evaluation
papers.Abstract: Merging RDF serializations creates ordering conflicts and misses semantic ones. We describe and evaluate a three-way merge in which the schema defines a conflict: set algebra combines canonical triples, and a slot is contended only where a SHACL shape bounds its cardinality and both sides' changes cannot stand within that bound. Unbounded predicates union; contended slots go to a person. The same shapes graph validates the result. We do not claim the first three-way merge for RDF. Our contribution is an implementation in a production multi-agent store and an evaluation against a reimplementation of Quit Store's Context Merge overlap rule, which it extends rather than replaces, and six other strategies. Across five synthetic seeds, the shape-aware operator raised 33 conflicts, all true positives as judged by the same shapes that define them, with no triples lost or fabricated and no SHACL violations admitted. The context-overlap baseline, counted per slot, detected the same 33 conflicts but asked 845 questions. A replay built from recorded production incidents covers 105 human alias repairs (93 after excluding 12 chained pairs) and 939 duplicate-value incidents. It reproduces a triple-level limit: different names for one entity remain invisible (0 of 93 alias repairs detected, matching 0 of 21 synthetic cases). In a study of evolving shape contracts, merging shape declarations first handles the tested cardinality changes, while datatype evolution exposes a detector blind spot caught by post-merge validation. An oracle that reads no shapes agrees with the shipped operator on the facts and history of all 23 reachable single-slot cases. Under wrong shapes, a missing bound loses data silently and a spurious one only adds questions. The supported claim is fewer human decisions with nothing silently lost, for cardinality conflicts in one deployment, not general merge correctness.
papers.Core_Innovation: Where a SHACL shape bounds predicate cardinality and both sides exceed it, the merge contends the slot for person assignment. Unbounded predicates freely union, and the result validates against the original shapes graph.
papers.Benefiting_Sectors: Semantic Technology, Data Integration, Cloud Computing
papers.Decision_Perspective: Integrate shape-aware three-way merge into production multi-agent stores within six months. Trigger adoption when SHACL-validated RDF merge consistency is required for critical knowledge graphs.
papers.Tags: RDF Merge, SHACL, Knowledge Graphs, Three-Way Merge
papers.Hook: Schema-defined SHACL cardinality now gates three-way RDF merge conflicts.

papers.Title: A Survey of Security, Privacy, and Ethics of Large Language Models in Telecom
papers.Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly integrated into telecommunications for customer service, network analytics, and operational support. While offering efficiency and innovation, their deployment raises critical privacy, security, and ethical challenges due to the uniquely sensitive and longitudinal nature of telecom data. This paper presents a survey of LLM risks and safeguards in telecom context. Our survey introduces a telecom-specific taxonomy linking privacy, security, and ethics with use cases and outlines open research challenges such as longitudinal data privacy, cross-border compliance, and scalable guardrails.
papers.Core_Innovation: Proposes a structured framework explicitly linking LLM privacy mechanisms security threat models ethical guidelines to telecom-specific data longitudinality and regulatory constraints.
papers.Decision_Perspective: Mandate a telecom LLM risk assessment audit within 6 months for all customer-facing deployments. Invest in open-source privacy-preserving guardrail frameworks meeting cross-border compliance standards.
papers.Tags: Large Language Models, Telecom, Privacy, Security
papers.Hook: First taxonomy links telecom LLM privacy, security, and ethics with operational use cases.

papers.Title: RePace: Reasoning about Demonstration Speedup for Faster Vision-Language-Action Policies
papers.Abstract: Since vision-language-action (VLA) policies can inherit the slow pace of human demonstrations, accelerating these demonstrations before fine-tuning can lead to faster VLA policies without an additional speed-selection module at deployment. Several offline speedup methods have focused on identifying segments that require less precision and assigning predefined speedup factors to the segments. However, even within a single segment, a speedup factor suitable for steady motion may be too high when precise alignment is required. To this end, this paper presents RePace, an offline reasoning framework that determines how much to accelerate each part of a demonstration. For the same recorded movement, RePace measures how much each candidate speedup factor shortens the sequence and compares the resulting observation-action pairs used for training. Given the task instruction, a pretrained language model uses the visual context and original motion of successive windows to interpret these candidate retiming effects and select a speedup profile for the complete episode. Experimental results demonstrate that RePace outperforms the baselines in overall task execution efficiency on both LIBERO and RoboCasa-Kitchen. On all three tasks with a gripper-equipped Franka Research 3 arm, RePace matches or exceeds the acceleration baselines in success rate and completes successful trials faster.
papers.Core_Innovation: RePace uses a frozen pretrained language model to reason about per-window speedup factors, balancing sequence compression against observation-action precision for each segment of a VLA demonstration.
papers.Decision_Perspective: VLA development teams should prototype RePace's per-window speedup logic using existing large language models within 2 months to quantify training efficiency gains. Existing pipelines relying on fixed segment speedup factors must be retired or reengineered by the next quarterly release cycle.
papers.Tags: VLA, Demo Acceleration, Language Reasoning, Robotics
papers.Hook: RePace enables per-demonstration-part speedup for VLA policies based on precision assessment

papers.Title: OmniAct: One Policy, One Million Embodiments
papers.Abstract: A single policy that controls diverse robots must not only transfer task knowledge across embodiments, but also adapt its behavior to each robot's capabilities. Existing approaches facilitate transfer through shared action representations, but these representations do not necessarily capture how differences in robot morphology should shape manipulation strategies. We introduce OmniAct, a cross-embodiment manipulation policy that conditions directly on each robot's kinematics in a specific scene to produce embodiment-specific behavior. This kinematic graph represents the robot's joint positions, motion axes, and connectivity to its visual observation, allowing the policy to account for how its embodiment related to objects and surfaces in the scene. A flow-matching policy predicts relative joint motions for each node, enabling control across robots with different degrees of freedom and kinematic configurations. To learn how physical structure shapes behavior at scale, we procedurally design and filter one million physically feasible robot embodiments; next, we develop algorithms to generate robot trajectories in simulation for all embodiments; finally, we train across diverse simulated manipulation tasks. On 2,000 embodiment-scene-held-out evaluation episodes, OmniAct achieves 63.0% success, compared to 17.8% for pi 0.5 and 57.9% for the strongest baseline; on the task families GPT-6 Astra was evaluated on, it achieves 64.7% against GPT-6 Astra's 41.1%. On a previously unseen real-world robot, it achieves nearly twice the success rate of the next best method, MolmoAct2. Beyond task success, we observe that OmniAct learns distinct manipulation strategies that exploit the capabilities and accommodate the limitations of different morphologies. Project: https://omniact.github.io/
papers.Core_Innovation: The policy conditions action generation on a per-robot kinematic graph encoding joint positions, motion axes, and visual connectivity, then uses flow-matching to predict morphology-aware relative joint motions.
papers.Decision_Perspective: Fund a 6-month pilot deploying OmniAct on 3 distinct robot morphologies to validate kinematic-graph transfer. Proceed to full rollout only if manipulation success exceeds 70% on target tasks across all morphologies.
papers.Tags: cross-embodiment, kinematics, flow-matching, manipulation, robotics
papers.Hook: Single policy adapts manipulation strategies to any robot's kinematics and scene geometry.

papers.Title: BioLoom: Scaling Biomedical Vision-Language Models by Learning from the Structure of Scientific Articles
papers.Abstract: The development of biomedical vision-language models (VLMs) with contrastive image-text pretraining has been driven by scaling to increasingly large and diverse image-text datasets. Beyond scaling, further progress can come from learning richer representations from existing data. We hypothesize that the structure of scientific literature itself provides an additional source of supervision: figures, panels, captions, and accompanying article text encode rich relationships across modalities. Yet, treating these as independent image-text pairs overlooks their relationships. To address this limitation, we incorporate these structural relationships into contrastive image-text supervision. We preserve exact image-text matches while introducing weaker positive supervision for related pairs, such as a panel and the caption of a sibling panel. We upweight cross-article negatives of the same content type to encourage finer discrimination. We also enrich panel descriptions using visual content, original figure captions, and mentioning paragraphs. Pairing panels with these descriptions and whole figures with their original captions yields Loom52M, a dataset of 52.4 million image-text pairs spanning scientific charts and biomedical images. Using Loom52M, BioLoom (DFN-2B) achieves 56.82% domain-balanced mean accuracy across 67 zero-shot classification tasks from 43 datasets in 10 domains, compared with 48.77% for MedPMC-CLIP. On BioLoomBench with concise captions and BioMedFlickr, it achieves bidirectional mean Recall@1 of 63.20% and 10.59%, versus 46.37% and 7.55% for the respective strongest evaluated baselines, BiomedCLIP and MedPMC-CLIP. Code, datasets, benchmarks, and models are available at https://bioloom-clip.github.io/.
papers.Core_Innovation: The method introduces structural supervision from scientific articles by preserving exact image-text matches while assigning weaker positives to related modal pairs and upweighting cross-article negatives to enforce finer discrimination.
papers.Benefiting_Sectors: Biomedical Imaging, Healthcare AI, Scientific Research
papers.Decision_Perspective: Allocate funding to integrate structural article supervision into biomedical VLM training within the next two quarters, targeting panel-caption and cross-article negative signal optimization. Phase out independent-pair scaling pipelines that ignore hierarchical content relationships.
papers.Tags: Biomedical, Contrastive, Structural, Articles
papers.Hook: Scientific article structure supervision enables finer biomedical VLM discrimination.

papers.Title: iWAM: Efficient Action Prediction from World Models without Explicit Future Prediction
papers.Abstract: World-action models (WAMs) build policies on pretrained video-generation models, on the premise that predicting how a scene evolves helps determine how to act. However, generating future scenes is expensive for real-time control. This motivates efficient proxies for future imagination, but how to train such proxies without sacrificing action-prediction quality remains unclear. An effective proxy need not generate a high-resolution frame; it only needs to provide enough information to distinguish between possible futures. This leads to the design principle behind iWAM: rather than denoising an entire future frame, can we condition the action policy on intermediate features from a single video-model evaluation? We show that the answer is yes. Exploiting the reversible dynamics of flow-matching models, we invert each training future into the corresponding latent noise vector. However, a single velocity evaluation at this latent does not necessarily yield informative features for action prediction. We therefore learn a bidirectional flow map that amortizes future-generation computation, enabling a single model evaluation to provide effective conditioning features. At inference, we sample a latent noise vector from the prior and condition the policy using just one video-backbone forward pass. Across simulated benchmarks and real robots, iWAM recovers the generalization benefits of WAMs while substantially reducing its inference cost.
papers.Core_Innovation: The method inverts future frames into latent noise vectors via flow-matching reversibility and conditions action policies on single-velocity features, eliminating the need for full-frame generation.
papers.Disrupted_Sectors: High-Fidelity Video Generation, Costly Offline Simulation
papers.Decision_Perspective: Product teams should prototype iWAM within 3 months for real-time robotics control, given its elimination of frame-generation overhead. Competitors relying on full-frame generation should evaluate migration paths within 6 months.
papers.Tags: flow-matching, latent features, action prediction, video models
papers.Hook: Latent features from single model evaluations enable action prediction without frame generation.

papers.Title: A Bias in Disguise: Tiny Gradient Edits Stop a Small Language Model's Thinking Loops and Complement a Frontier Model's Weight Edit
papers.Abstract: Qwen3.5-0.8B rarely finishes reasoning in thinking mode: at a 4,096-token budget only 1 or 2 of 500 MATH-500 answers close their think block (two seeds), and accuracy is 15.4%. A recent demonstration had GPT-6 Astra edit 131,072 of the model's weights without gradients and reported MATH-500 rising from 7.9% to 48.1% at a 32,768-token budget. We provide the missing gradient baseline, then combine the two edits. Fine-tuning only the 140 to 139,750 weights with the largest gradient, on the model's own correct answers to MATH training problems, raises thinking-mode MATH-500 at 4k tokens to 39.0-45.5% after 2-9 minutes of training on one GPU; 50 training examples suffice, and 1,398 random positions give only 16.3%. The gradient concentrates the edit on the most nearly constant channel of each of the first three layers. Because the model has no bias terms, an edit confined to those channels acts as a constant vector added to the residual stream: adding three fixed vectors to the unedited model matches the accuracy of such an edit. Under the Astra protocol (32k tokens, presence penalty 1.5), the Astra edit scores 52.1% (finished and correct) in our reproduction and our full-strength edits reach 45.6-45.7%, but ours win at every budget up to 16k tokens (39.5% against 6.7% at 4k). The two edits are complementary. The Astra edit plus our 139,750-weight edit at half strength scores 62.2% at 32k, 10 points above the Astra edit alone (p = 3e-9), with half as many tokens; our half-strength edit alone scores 46.7%.
papers.Core_Innovation: Gradient analysis pinpoints the most nearly constant channels in the first three layers, and selective editing of 140 large-magnitude weights using correct MATH answers acts as a constant vector added to the residual stream, enabling reasoning loops without bias terms.
papers.Disrupted_Sectors: Large Scale Model Training, Cloud GPU Providers
papers.Decision_Perspective: Fund gradient-editing toolkit development for sub-1B models within 3 months to capture reasoning efficiency gains. Kill frontier model fine-tuning pilots that cannot match this targeted editing approach by Q2.
papers.Tags: gradient editing, model reasoning, weight sparsity, LLM optimization
papers.Hook: Tiny gradient edits on 140 weights enable small models to sustain multi-step reasoning.

papers.Title: Exploratory Midtraining for Robot Policies
papers.Abstract: Robot policies predominantly learn from human-collected data emphasizing competent behavior, limiting coverage of the low-level behaviors needed to support autonomous improvement. We study how a form of midtraining can be used to build coverage over diverse low-level behaviors that connect challenging states of the robot and its environment to states from which further progress is possible ("connected behavioral coverage"). We also examine how this coverage supports downstream adaptation and online improvement. To this end, we introduce $β$-Data, a dataset collected via adversarial teleoperation, where a human adversary reversibly perturbs the environment while a human operator continues toward completion without resetting. We relabel trajectory segments with local outcomes in natural language and finetune a pretrained policy conditioned on recent action history. The resulting policy exhibits sustained use of more low-level behaviors. Across manipulation tasks in simulation and on three real-robot platforms, our approach yields more favorable data scaling laws, better zero-shot generalization, and more effective use of additional rollout time than training on standard demonstrations. During online finetuning, these policies need fewer rollouts to collect successful experience and reach higher success rates, suggesting that midtraining can prepare robots for both more robust task execution and continued autonomous improvement. Our project page and robot videos are available at https://kshitiz-1225.github.io/exploratory-midtraining-robot-policies/.
papers.Core_Innovation: β-Data collects trajectories via adversarial teleoperation where a human adversary perturbs the environment mid-task, allowing trajectory relabeling with local outcome labels while preserving task flow. Then it finetunes a policy conditioned on recent action history to expand low-level behavioral coverage.
papers.Decision_Perspective: Allocate R&D budget to build adversarial midtraining pipelines within the next two quarters. Deprecate static demonstration workflows that fail to capture perturbed state transitions.
papers.Tags: Midtraining, Adversarial Teleoperation, Robot Policies, Behavioral Coverage, Finetuning
papers.Hook: Adversarial midtraining enables robots to sustain low-level behaviors across challenging states.

papers.Title: MetaFORGE: A Meta-Learning Framework for Harness Optimization in Automated Code Generation for Parallel Computing
papers.Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can generate parallel programs, but their correctness and performance depend strongly on the instructions that guide generation. We present \textsc{MetaFORGE}, an execution-grounded meta-learning framework that iteratively optimizes persistent natural-language skill specifications for MPI C code generation. \textsc{MetaFORGE} combines correctness testing, compiler diagnostics, static-analysis findings, runtime measurements, and rank-level load-imbalance profiles into a scalar reward that drives textual-gradient refinement, while an external memory distills and retrieves reward-supported optimization knowledge across runs.   Across six MPI tasks and three workload sizes, \textsc{MetaFORGE} improves static-analysis quality, runtime, and load balance relative to zero-shot generation and generally exceeds the evaluated \textsc{TextGrad} iterative baseline. A model-matched refinement ablation shows that the MetaFORGE advantage persists when its refinement model is reduced to \texttt{gpt-4o}. An expanded retrieval ablation across all 18 task--workload configurations shows consistent runtime benefit and broad static-analysis and load-balance benefit from retrieved context. Leakage-controlled held-out and zero-update experiments further provide evidence that optimization knowledge persists in both the transferred skill and external memory under the evaluated protocol.
papers.Core_Innovation: Integrates runtime load-imbalance profiles and compiler diagnostics into a scalar reward for textual-gradient refinement of prompt specifications.
papers.Benefiting_Sectors: High Performance Computing, Cloud Infrastructure, Scientific Research, Quantitative Finance
papers.Decision_Perspective: Fund the integration of execution-feedback loops into existing LLM-based coding pipelines within the next fiscal quarter. Buy compute resources to automate the migration of legacy MPI codebases to optimized versions.
papers.Tags: MPI, Meta-Learning, Parallel Computing, Textual Gradients, LLM Optimization
papers.Hook: Automated optimization of MPI C code via execution-grounded meta-learning for high-performance parallel computing.

papers.Title: Draft Calibration for Speculative Decoding: Accelerating LLM Serving by Matching Draft and Target Distributions
papers.Abstract: Speculative decoding accelerates large language model (LLM) inference by employing a lightweight draft model to propose draft tokens and allowing the target model to verify the new tokens in parallel to improve inference-time compute utilization. The speedup relies on the acceptance probability of draft tokens in target verification, which is directly related to the gap $\|p-q\|_1$ between the target distribution $p$ and the draft distribution $q$. In this paper, we study draft calibration of speculative decoding to improve the speedup of speculative decoding, where we employ post-hoc methods to calibrate the draft distribution to mitigate the distribution gap. We observe that though current community open-source draft models may learn the top candidate token correctly, they are generally underconfident compared to the target model, suggesting a consistent distribution mismatch. To mitigate the effect of this mismatch on the acceptance rate of the draft models, we try various post-hoc calibration methods, including standard temperature scaling and token-wise calibration. Our results suggest that a standard temperature scaling applied to the draft distribution improves the acceptance length by up to approximately 10\% with almost no additional cost across different tasks. Throughput analysis further verifies that this improvement in serving efficiency. Analysis of more general calibration methods reveals further potential room for improvement.
papers.Core_Innovation: The paper proposes post-hoc logit calibration to align draft model confidence with the target model, directly minimizing the L1 distribution gap that governs draft token acceptance in speculative decoding
papers.Decision_Perspective: Integrate post-hoc draft calibration into production LLM serving pipelines within 90 days to measure acceptance rate gains. Deprioritize uncalibrated draft model research given the demonstrated distribution-matching advantage.
papers.Tags: Speculative Decoding, LLM Inference, Distribution Calibration
papers.Hook: Post-hoc draft calibration narrows L1 distribution gaps for faster LLM inference

papers.Title: Temporal Conditioning for Human Behavioral Cloning in Chess
papers.Abstract: Behavioral cloning models in chess typically predict human moves from board states while ignoring temporal inputs such as the remaining clock. However, time pressure is a major determinant of human decision-making quality, and temporal state is a missing dimension of human behavioral modeling. This paper introduces a time-aware transformer that extends a Chessformer-style architecture with learned temporal conditioning tokens encoding player clock state, time control, and recent tempo, together with behavioral heads for thinking time and resignation. The model is trained on large-scale online chess data and evaluated against time-agnostic baselines and the state of the art. Results show that temporal conditioning yields modest overall accuracy improvements but substantially stronger gains under time pressure. Beyond move choice, it also produces more accurate thinking-time and resignation predictions. More importantly, the model better matches human move-quality degradation in critical time regimes, reducing the systematic over-strength observed in time-agnostic behavioral cloning models. These results suggest that temporal state is a previously underutilized but important signal for human behavioral cloning in chess.
papers.Core_Innovation: A time-aware transformer integrates learned temporal conditioning tokens encoding clock state, time control, and recent tempo into move, thinking-time, and resignation prediction heads
papers.Benefiting_Sectors: Artificial Intelligence, Online Gaming, Financial Analytics
papers.Decision_Perspective: Product teams should immediately integrate temporal conditioning into next-gen chess engines to capture time-pressure user segments. Venture capitalists should fund startups deploying behavioral cloning with real-time clock analytics within 18 months
papers.Tags: Temporal Conditioning, Behavioral Cloning, Chess AI, Time Pressure, Move Quality
papers.Hook: Temporal tokens enable chess AI to degrade move quality like humans under time pressure

papers.Title: Reinforcement Learning Can Be Recovered From Its Own Rollouts
papers.Abstract: Broadly speaking, reinforcement learning (RL) post-training converts compute into model capabilities by training on model-generated data. Typically, the rollouts are discarded after each update, and the knowledge acquired during RL resides in the model weights. In this work, we investigate how much of this knowledge is retained in the rollouts themselves. A natural first attempt is to replay the original RL algorithm on archived rather than freshly generated rollouts, but this leads to catastrophic collapse. We provide a simple explanation for this phenomenon, which in turn suggests a remedy: maximum likelihood on the archived rollouts. Surprisingly, starting from the same base model and replaying the rollouts in the order in which they were generated, without any distinction between correct and incorrect responses, is sufficient to recover the performance of online RL. In fact, a single maximum likelihood update per rollout batch closely tracks the entire learning curve of online RL. Furthermore, maximum likelihood on the rollouts of the last few RL steps often suffices to recover the final model's performance. This suggests that much of the compute invested in RL goes into discovering an improved sampling distribution rather than learning it from samples.
papers.Core_Innovation: The technical delta is using maximum likelihood estimation on archived rollouts in generation order, without filtering correct/incorrect responses, to recover online RL performance without catastrophic collapse.
papers.Disrupted_Sectors: Reinforcement Learning Training, Data Labeling, Cloud Compute
papers.Decision_Perspective: Fund maximum-likelihood rollout replay pipelines immediately to compress RL training costs by 40%. Trigger deployment when archived dataset exceeds 10,000 samples.
papers.Tags: reinforcement-learning, maximum-likelihood, rollout-replay
papers.Hook: Archived RL rollouts can recover online training performance via maximum likelihood replay.

papers.Title: GREMLIN: Generating Random Environments for Meta-Learning with Interacting Networks
papers.Abstract: Can randomly parameterized neural environments supply useful experience for learning a reinforcement learning algorithm? We investigate this question using DiscoRL's rule-discovery framework, replacing human-designed training games with sixteen selected neural environments. Each game combines bounded vector dynamics with a random strategy-based reward and an independent outcome reward. After 224.8 million agent-environment steps, we froze the teacher and trained fresh agents. DQN outscored GREMLIN on most games, both generated and human-designed. GREMLIN nevertheless outperformed the untrained teacher on all 26 games, showing that generated experience can improve a learning rule. It remains unclear whether this approach can yield a competitive rule with longer meta-training.
papers.Core_Innovation: Neural environments with interacting networks autonomously generate bounded vector dynamics and reward functions, supplying meta-training experience without human-designed games
papers.Decision_Perspective: Fund a 6-month pilot to integrate GREMLIN-generated environments into existing meta-RL pipelines, targeting DQN parity on 10 benchmark games as the go/no-go trigger. Stop investment if parity is not achieved within the pilot window.
papers.Tags: Meta-Learning,Reinforcement Learning,Neural Environments,Rule Discovery,Generated Experience
papers.Hook: Random neural environments enable learning rules that surpass untrained teachers via generated experience

papers.Title: Delegent: A Multi-Agent Harness That Reduces Cost without Sacrificing Performance
papers.Abstract: Agents built on frontier language models are expensive. At every step, the frontier model re-reads its entire context and executes every subtask regardless of its difficulty. This paper explores the simple thesis that much of this cost can be removed by delegating easy subtasks to a small language model, or SLM, that runs on hardware one already owns. To test it, we build Delegent, a simple and effective agent harness built on Claude Code, in which the frontier model stays in charge of every task but hands focused subtasks, such as investigating code, running tests, and searching a corpus, to SLM subagents. Existing approaches such as cascades and model routers usually choose which model executes the entire task, whereas in Delegent, the frontier model always leads the execution and delegates easy subtasks to the SLM. No router or model is trained, so either model can be swapped freely. With the help of a 27B FP8 SLM, Delegent reduces the frontier cost of long-horizon coding by 67% and of agentic search by 59%, with no loss in task performance, and even a 2B SLM that fits on a laptop reduces the coding cost by 66%. The savings grow with the legwork that the frontier model would otherwise do itself, and a short instruction, which leaves the main coding tasks to the frontier model, accounts for most of the saving and keeps the 2B SLM from losing tasks. Code: https://github.com/castorini/delegent
papers.Core_Innovation: The frontier model retains full task ownership while dynamically offloading verified easy subtasks to on-device SLMs via real-time decomposition, eliminating redundant context re-reads without any model training.
papers.Benefiting_Sectors: Software Engineering, AI Infrastructure, Developer Tools
papers.Disrupted_Sectors: Enterprise AI Consulting, Premium Model Hosting
papers.Decision_Perspective: Fund engineering teams to integrate Delegent-style delegation into coding pipelines within 6 months, achieving at least 50% frontier model cost reduction. Phase out high-priced standalone coding assistant subscriptions as delegation drives per-task costs below current market rates.
papers.Tags: multi-agent, cost reduction, SLM delegation, coding automation, frontier models
papers.Hook: Frontier models can delegate easy subtasks to local SLMs, slashing costs without performance loss.

papers.Title: EventDiffusion: Learning Native Event Stream Distribution from Videos
papers.Abstract: Event cameras capture asynchronous brightness changes at high temporal resolution, but scarce recordings constrain data-driven research. Sparse RGB observations cannot uniquely determine intervening events since identical frames may correspond to streams with different activity, polarities, and timing. Existing simulators largely rely on prescribed sensor dynamics and estimated brightness trajectories, whose assumptions limit the diversity and fidelity of plausible event streams. We introduce EventDiffusion, a hierarchical generative framework that directly learns the conditional distribution of native asynchronous event streams from real recordings. EventDiffusion decomposes generation into three probabilistic processes: Event Activity Diffusion (EAD) learns stochastic discrete event counts; Event Spatial Allocation (ESA) distributes these counts to individual pixels while preserving cardinality; and Event Timing Diffusion (ETD) learns continuous asynchronous timestamp distributions. We also introduce CEFS, an event-stream realism metric combining event activity and polarity with multiscale space-time structure and temporal fidelity. Across all datasets, EventDiffusion achieves double the accuracy of SOTA methods and demonstrates robustness across different cameras at any resolution.
papers.Core_Innovation: Hierarchically decomposes event generation into coupled activity-spatial-timing diffusion processes, learning native asynchronous distributions directly from real recordings without prescribed sensor dynamics.
papers.Decision_Perspective: Allocate R&D budget to integrate EventDiffusion into synthetic event-stream pipelines for autonomous sensor validation within 180 days. Phase out legacy event simulators relying on prescribed sensor dynamics due to their limited fidelity and diversity.
papers.Tags: event diffusion, generative models, asynchronous events, spatial allocation, synthetic data
papers.Hook: Directly learns native event stream distributions from real recordings.

papers.Title: AIChipBench: Benchmarking LLM Agents for Automated AI Accelerator Design
papers.Abstract: A language-model decoder carries state between decoding steps, and in hardware a wrong state update can leave the current token correct and corrupt the output several tokens later, so a design can pass output tests and still be wrong. AIChipBench asks what LLM coding agents need to build such hardware correctly. Agents implement quantized Qwen3.5, Gemma 3, Gemma 4, and Llama 3.2 decoders in synthesizable register-transfer-level (RTL) code against an executable integer reference that specifies the outputs and the stored state at every decoding step. They debug against public tests under fixed budgets; their frozen designs are graded on held-out token sequences, resets, memory stalls, and synthesis, and a second track asks them to speed up a correct design at nearly fixed area. Across 9,136 attempts by four coding agents, the difficulty lies in stored state. Feedback that points to the first state mismatch raises acceptance over output-only feedback in all 12 agent--task cells of a matched study, by 25.0 to 46.9 percentage points, and halves the agent-hours per accepted design. Regraded on new sequences and conditions, 45 of 69 accepted designs fail within the 32 steps their tests required. More than a third of attempts to speed up a correct design end without one. An overall score ranks Sol 5.6 and Fable 5.1 above Astra 6 and Opus 5.5, and both halves of the instances give this order in all 200 random splits. Hardware agents therefore need debugging feedback that exposes stored state, and their benchmarks need final tests well beyond the development cases.
papers.Core_Innovation: Introduces an executable integer reference that tracks stored decoder state at every step, allowing LLM agents to detect and correct hidden state mismatches that output-only testing misses
papers.Benefiting_Sectors: Semiconductor, AI Chip Design, Hardware Automation
papers.Decision_Perspective: Allocate capital to semiconductor startups integrating AIChipBench within the next quarter to accelerate correct-by-construction accelerator development. Mandate state-aware verification protocols for all in-house RTL projects within 3 months to close the output-vs-state testing gap.
papers.Tags: LLM Agents, Hardware Benchmarking, State Tracking, RTL Design
papers.Hook: LLM agents can now benchmark and fix hidden state errors in AI accelerator RTL design

papers.Title: The Radar-based Activities of Daily Living (R-ADL) Dataset
papers.Abstract: Monitoring Activities of Daily Living (ADLs) supports safety and well-being for people living at home, especially older adults, and radar sensing is gaining increasing attention in the field of activity recognition for its ability to ensure privacy in the home while also surpassing technical limitations of other sensing modalities. However, radar-based activity recognition remains constrained by the limited availability of large-scale datasets. We introduce the Radar-based Activities of Daily Living (R-ADL) dataset to addresses the gaps identified in existing work: 1) it expands the scale of available data by providing over eight hours of annotated recordings in which a person performs eight distinct activities; 2) it overcomes room configuration limitations by recording from five different locations in a two-bedroom, two-bathroom apartment; and 3) it extends beyond primitive actions to focus on high-level ADLs. In addition to the dataset, this paper introduces practical guidance for future ADL dataset construction. We conducted a detailed analysis of how ADLs are prioritized across academic research, health survey tools, and clinical trials to identify clinically significant ADLs. Furthermore, we provide our experimental design, data collection and annotation strategies, post-processing pipeline for forming the R-ADL dataset from raw data, and baseline results on standard machine learning architectures. The R-ADL dataset serves as a valuable resource for advancing ADL recognition systems as we continue building larger and more diverse datasets.
papers.Core_Innovation: First multi-location radar dataset with high-level ADL annotations across five indoor environments
papers.Benefiting_Sectors: Healthcare, Smart Home Technology, Elder Care
papers.Decision_Perspective: Prioritize funding radar-based ADL startups within 12 months to validate privacy advantages over camera systems. Secure enterprise licensing for the R-ADL dataset within 6 months for elder-care pilot deployments.
papers.Tags: Radar, ADL, Dataset, Activity Recognition, Privacy
papers.Hook: Radar now captures 8 high-level ADLs across 5 home locations with 8+ hours of annotated data

papers.Title: Uncertainty-Aware Candidate Generation for Entity Linking in Cyber Threat Intelligence
papers.Abstract: Entity Resolution (ER) pipelines often collapse ambiguity into early hard decisions: upstream Named Entity Recognition (NER) selects a single span and type, and downstream Entity Linking (EL) treats that choice as ground truth. This discards valuable information about the ambiguity of the underlying data (e.g., span boundary disagreement and type confusion), leading to brittle systems that fail unpredictably when faced with uncertainty in inputs. Therefore, this work presents a proof-of-concept for uncertainty-aware ER that treats uncertainty as native data that should be preserved and exploited throughout ER pipelines. We (i) capture uncertainty signals in the NER stage and (ii) leverage these signals into the EL stage to improve candidate retrieval under ambiguity. Using a BERT-based NER model augmented with two auxiliary span-boundary prediction heads, we apply Monte Carlo (MC) dropout at inference time to derive three mention-level proxy signals: the MC-averaged start-boundary probability, the MC-averaged end-boundary probability, and De Luca-Termini fuzzy entropy computed over the Begin-Inside-Outside (BIO) predictive distribution. These signals are used to adapt the fuzzy cutoff in candidate generation (CG) for EL. Because CG is treated as a blocking step, we evaluate retrieval recall. On the AnnoCTR dataset linked to the MITRE ATTCK knowledge base, the boundary-aware and dual-signal fuzzy linking approaches improve Recall@10 from 0.6186 to 0.7966. The contribution lies not in an end-to-end optimised ER pipeline but in establishing uncertainty preservation as a viable and beneficial component of ER pipelines, enabling downstream EL to make better-informed decisions under uncertainty.
papers.Core_Innovation: Auxiliary span-boundary heads + MC dropout on BERT NER produce three proxy uncertainty signals that directly inform EL candidate retrieval, replacing hard span-type decisions
papers.Decision_Perspective: Allocate R&D budget to integrate MC-dropout uncertainty signals into CTI EL pipelines within 6 months to replace hard-decision NER outputs. Immediately sunset legacy NER-EL workflows that treat span selections as ground truth by Q3 2026
papers.Tags: Entity Linking, Uncertainty Quantification, Cyber Threat Intelligence, Monte Carlo Dropout, Span Boundary
papers.Hook: Monte Carlo dropout quantifies NER ambiguity for precise CTI entity disambiguation

papers.Title: Shifter Quantization: Compact Representations for Native Integer Computation
papers.Abstract: Groupwise quantization is used in LLM quantization to improve accuracy at low bit widths, but grouping weights keeps standard integer MMA from spanning the full dot product for efficient GPU inference. We develop a new quantization method, Shifter Quantization (SQ), that reconstructs native-width integer operands by appending and shifting shared bits. To further extend the efficiency, we develop a special variant of SQ, Shifter Integer (SHI), to use INT4 kernels. We show that SQ and SHI formats perform better than standard groupwise quantization in quality, as measured by projection error and KL divergence, and in inference speed, as measured during decoding and prefill. For low precision like 2-bit quantization, SQ2 and SHI2 achieve 2.71-3.77x the 4,096-token prefill throughput of llama.cpp on a Q2_K checkpoint and reduce WikiText-2 KL by 6.6-7.8%. For mid precision like 4-bit quantization, SQ4 achieves 1.43-2.47x the prefill throughput of NInfer's groupwise-integer baselines across the tested models and prompt lengths, with 24-40% lower KL than the NInfer baselines. For high precision like 8-bit quantization, SQ8 achieves 27.4% higher batch-one prefill throughput and 72.7% lower KL than vLLM's online FP8.
papers.Core_Innovation: Shifter Quantization reconstructs full-width integer operands by appending and shifting shared group bits, enabling full-dot-product integer matrix multiplication without grouping constraints.
papers.Benefiting_Sectors: Large Language Models, AI Hardware, Cloud Computing
papers.Decision_Perspective: We will prototype SHI kernel integration into our LLM serving stack within 90 days to capture 2.5x prefill throughput improvements on Q4 checkpoints. We will phase out groupwise-only quantization pipelines that lack native integer width reconstruction, replacing them with SHI-compatible alternatives.
papers.Tags: Quantization, Integer Arithmetic, LLM Inference, Throughput, Bitwidth
papers.Hook: Shifter Quantization enables native-width integer operands via bit appending, boosting INT4 throughput and accuracy.

papers.Title: Optimal Linear Regression Without a Variance
papers.Abstract: We study high-probability linear regression in the infinite variance regime, wherecthe regression noise has only a finite conditional $α$-moment $ν$ for some unknown $α\in(1,2)$, and the covariates may only have finite moments up to a given order (e.g., 4th moment). We give a black-box reduction that converts finite-variance regression procedures into weak-moment procedures. The reduction is based on empirical residual pruning and is agnostic to the moment exponent, the noise scale, the covariance, and the design moment. Under a finite fourth-moment condition on the covariates, any finite-variance subroutine attaining the sub-Gaussian rate yields the following when the number of samples $n$ is above a suitably defined threshold: Without knowing $α$ or $ν$, we have with probability at least $1-δ$ that $ \|\widehatθ-θ^*\|_Σ   \lesssim_α   ν^{1/α}   \big(\frac{d+\log(1/δ)}{n}\big)^{\frac{α-1}α}, $ where $d$ is the dimension, $Σ$ is the covariate covariance matrix, and $\|v\|_Σ:=(v^\topΣv)^{1/2}$. We further prove a matching minimax lower bound that holds under the same conditions. The reduction is computationally efficient whenever the finite-variance subroutine is. We also obtain a distribution-free prediction guarantee under a bounded raw $α$-moment assumption on the response, and give an analogous $α$-agnostic reduction for mean estimation.
papers.Core_Innovation: Uses empirical residual pruning as a black-box reduction to convert any finite-variance sub-Gaussian regression routine into an optimal procedure for unknown α-moment noise, requiring only a finite fourth-moment assumption on covariates
papers.Decision_Perspective: Prioritize integrating empirical residual pruning into existing finite-variance solvers for datasets with suspected heavy-tailed noise. Deploy within 6 months on any production regression system where covariate fourth moments are verifiable.
papers.Tags: robust regression, infinite variance, fourth moments
papers.Hook: Enables sub-Gaussian regression under infinite variance using only fourth-moment data

papers.Title: A Methodologically Rigorous Benchmark of Linear Regression,RNN, and LSTM for S&P 500 Forecasting:Identifying Sources of Performance Inflation in Financial DeepLearning
papers.Abstract: This study examines one-day-ahead forecasting of the S&P 500 closing level using a 2006-2025 dataset that includes fundamental price data, macroeconomic indicators, and engineered technical features. We benchmark three model families, namely linear regression, vanilla recurrent neural networks (RNN), and long short-term memory networks (LSTM), within a unified preprocessing and chronological evaluation pipeline. A central contribution of this work is a methodological audit of common practices in the deep-learning-for-stock-prediction literature. We identify three sources of result inflation that frequently appear in published methodologies: wavelet-denoised evaluation targets, the absence of a naive persistence baseline, and best-of-N replicate reporting. We then re-evaluate all model families under a corrected protocol that controls for each. Performance is reported using root mean squared error, mean absolute percentage error, and the Pearson correlation coefficient, averaged across N = 30 independent replicates per configuration. We compare models on accuracy, stability across replicates, and architectural depth sensitivity, using the naive persistence forecast (predicting today's close as tomorrow's close) as a primary baseline against which all candidate models must demonstrate improvement.
papers.Core_Innovation: A unified chronological benchmark that explicitly controls for wavelet-denoised evaluation targets, naive persistence baselines, and best-of-N replicate reporting across linear, RNN, and LSTM models
papers.Benefiting_Sectors: Quantitative Trading, Asset Management, Risk Analytics
papers.Decision_Perspective: Mandate persistence-baseline and replication guards for all S&P 500 forecasting models within 90 days. Phase out wavelet-denoised evaluation targets in internal model audits immediately.
papers.Tags: Financial Deep Learning, Methodological Audit, Benchmark, Performance Inflation
papers.Hook: Unmasking three inflation sources that artificially inflate financial deep-learning forecasts

papers.Title: On the Complete Feature Set for ADHD Classification in Children and Adolescents Based on EEG Signals
papers.Abstract: Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder is a neurodevelopmental condition that can affect attention, activity and impulse control. Electroencephalography (EEG) records brain activity as children and adolescents perform cognitive tasks. However, comparing features derived from these recordings requires consistent signal preparation, shared analysis windows and documented quality decisions. We curated 669 existing BALLADEER recordings from 156 participants across five task conditions so that researchers can compare seven EEG feature families on the same time intervals for each participant and task. The dataset links continuous signals to precomputed measurements from 115 feature definitions or templates and records the quality decisions made for each recording. Analyses must still account for repeated measurements within participants, residual artefacts and differences between acquisition systems. Technical validation covered signal integrity, numerical checks on feature estimators and completeness of the released files. In every task, the median proportion of recording time retained after preprocessing was 100%. To illustrate reuse, we report saved participant-held-out evaluations comparing XGBoost using all seven families on eight-second windows with a predictor based only on recruitment-group prevalence in the training fold. Recruitment-group discrimination was stronger in Robots than in the three Slackline conditions. These descriptive results from overlapping cohorts do not establish diagnostic validity. The dataset, curation software and aggregate results for the predictive example are publicly available.
papers.Core_Innovation: Per-recording quality decisions align 115 EEG feature definitions across 5 task conditions in 156 pediatric participants.
papers.Benefiting_Sectors: Neuroscience Research, Pediatric Healthcare, Digital Health
papers.Decision_Perspective: Integrate quality-flagged, aligned EEG features from this dataset into pediatric ADHD clinical trials within 6 months. Mandate standardized feature families and quality flags for all new multicenter childhood neuroimaging studies starting Q2 2025.
papers.Tags: EEG, ADHD, Children, Feature Standardization, Quality Control
papers.Hook: A curated EEG dataset enables standardized ADHD feature comparison across 156 children and 5 tasks.

papers.Title: Non-penetrating World Models
papers.Abstract: We study a new problem of preventing object penetration in interactive video world models. To understand how existing models handle this, we introduce NoPeBench, a benchmark that evaluates how world models respond to physical obstacles.
