Numerical experiments in scientific modeling demonstrate the full learning pipeline and yield accurate predictors with few trainable parameters, using the model both for end-to-end prediction and within layers of larger architectures.
papers.Core_Innovation: Constructs equivariant polynomial features whose coefficients are learnable functions of minimal homogeneous invariant generators, with automated feature computation via explicit isotypic and Clebsch-Gordan decompositions of tensor products.
papers.Decision_Perspective: Allocate R&D budget to integrate minimal-generator equivariant feature pipelines into scientific simulation workflows within 18 months. Deprecate symmetry-agnostic polynomial feature pipelines in favor of this representation-aware approach.
papers.Tags: equivariant,polynomial features,invariant theory,computational algebra
papers.Hook: Minimal homogeneous generators enable automated equivariant polynomial feature construction.

papers.Title: On Evaluating User Simulators for Interactive Agents
papers.Abstract: User simulators offer a scalable way to evaluate interactive agents, but how to assess their quality remains underexplored. In particular, it is unclear whether existing user simulator evaluation frameworks reliably detect meaningful failures in simulated user behavior. This uncertainty makes it difficult to interpret simulator evaluation. To understand what a high benchmark score tells us about simulator quality, we (meta-)evaluate the metrics themselves. To instantiate this meta-evaluation, we deliberately perturb simulated replays to induce failures such as altered goals, omitted constraints, premature stopping, and acceptance of broken work, then test whether the metrics penalize these failures. Evaluation methods from three prior studies detect only 5-6 of the 10 perturbations; their combined scores even favor populations instructed to accept broken work over unmodified controls. Motivated by these gaps, we propose a new evaluation suite that combines utility of user simulators for evaluating agents and two measures of fidelity to real users: population-level fidelity assesses collective interaction patterns, while trace-level fidelity assesses the preservation of individual users' goals, constraints, and persona. Under the same detection criterion, our evaluation suite detects all 10 perturbations. Evaluating six user simulators on 351 real multi-turn sessions in which 348 distinct users across 23 languages and agents work together to create and refine artifacts such as full-stack web apps, games, design assets, and automated workflows, we find that population-level measures can miss when a simulated user pursues the wrong goal, ignores a constraint, or behaves out of character, highlighting the need to assess fidelity at comprehensive granularities.
papers.Core_Innovation: Perturbation-based meta-evaluation exposes blind spots in existing user simulator metrics by systematically inducing goal alterations, constraint omissions, premature stopping, and broken-work acceptance
papers.Decision_Perspective: Product teams should integrate the new perturbation-based evaluation suite within six months to replace existing user simulator metrics. Companies relying on unvalidated interactive agent benchmarks should audit and replace current metrics immediately.
papers.Tags: user simulators, interactive agents, evaluation metrics
papers.Hook: New evaluation suite reliably detects simulator failures missed by prior metrics

papers.Title: Cap-and-Track: Optimizing LLM Inference Request Dispatch Across Shifting Capacity
papers.Abstract: A fixed dispatch rate for LLM inference becomes stale as serving fleets resize and request sizes change. Generative output length is unknown at admission, and shared provider pools can lose capacity. We present Cap-and-Track, a design for asynchronous inference across provider capacity and internal GPUs. Meta's traffic shaper implements Cap-and-Track for post and live-video understanding. Refusals signal the backend's current admission ceiling. Durable priority queues hold excess work outside execution, including refused requests for retry. Cap is a fail-fast admission check at the saturated resource that refuses work before a long wait. Using only those refusals, the Track dispatcher probes upward and backs off. It follows the ceiling without output-length prediction or a fleet-level rate to retune. In a concurrent same-traffic production A/B, the shaper ran per-replica Cap plus Track. It served a classifier on 43% fewer H100s than its queued, fixed-rate precursor, though lower-priority work waited longer at backfill peaks. In steady-capacity real-engine replay, Track ran within 1% of the goodput of a fixed rate tuned above measured capacity, with about a quarter of that rate's refusal share. The shaper carries more than 300 million online requests and hundreds of terabytes of media a day. During a backfill, it handled 1.1 billion requests in its busiest 24 hours. Lessons include keeping queues inside inference engines just long enough to fill batches, steering dispatch by capacity refusals alone, keeping dispatch stateful, and sizing fleets by how long low-priority work can wait.
papers.Core_Innovation: Cap implements a fail-fast admission check that refuses work at saturated resources. Track uses only refusal signals to dynamically probe and adjust capacity, dispensing with output-length prediction and fixed fleet-wide rates.
papers.Benefiting_Sectors: Cloud Computing, Video Streaming, Artificial Intelligence
papers.Disrupted_Sectors: Traditional Queue Management, Over-Provisioned GPU Clusters, Fixed-Rate Dispatch Systems
papers.Decision_Perspective: Allocate R&D budget to integrate Cap-and-Track dispatch within 6 months to cut GPU procurement costs by 40%. Retire fixed-rate dispatchers in all new LLM deployments within 12 months as refusal-based admission becomes the performance standard.
papers.Tags: LLM inference, capacity dispatch, refusal signals, adaptive routing, GPU optimization
papers.Hook: LLM inference dispatches adaptively using refusal signals, eliminating need for output-length prediction.

papers.Title: Who are you? The Personal Imitation Game
papers.Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) now perform strongly on Alan Turing's 1950 Imitation Game, so we propose a harder challenge, the Personal Imitation Game, which asks whether a machine can replicate a specific individual in conversation rather than a generic human. Testing with 30 participants, we establish a human baseline and report the identity signals interrogators rely on: stylometric features, personality traits, and biographical facts. To demonstrate the framework, we design an LLM-based system that plays the game for one of the paper's authors, drawing on an autoethnographic dataset spanning ten years of personal digital communication. In a 20-person deception study, interrogators choose our system over the author's own friends in 7 of 10 rounds, and the author over our system in 13 of 20; neither rate is distinguishable from chance at this sample size. We consider design improvements, applications of personal AI agents, and implications for identity and privacy.
papers.Core_Innovation: A decade-long autoethnographic data pipeline extracts stylometric personality and biographical signals to prompt an LLM into specific persona conversation tested against human comparators in a deception game
papers.Disrupted_Sectors: Identity Verification, Social Media, Generic Chatbots
papers.Decision_Perspective: Allocate 6-month funding to prototype a personal AI agent using autoethnographic data pipelines triggered by proven consumer interest in digital identity preservation. Discontinue generic LLM deployments in customer service roles where identity mimicry risk exceeds 5% without explicit user consent
papers.Tags: Personal Imitation, Autoethnography, Stylometry, LLM Personalization, Identity Privacy
papers.Hook: LLMs can now mimic specific individuals in real-time conversation beyond generic human imitation

papers.Title: Monoculture Robust Learning
papers.Abstract: We introduce a notion of monoculture robustness in Probably Approximately Correct (PAC) learning, as a way to mitigate the problem of algorithmic monoculture (Kleinberg and Raghavan, 2021): the tendency of models sharing the same components (e.g., training data) to fail on the same inputs. Specifically, we ask whether a learner with access to a single dataset can output $k$ individually accurate hypotheses whose joint failure probability is comparable to training on $k$ independent datasets. We say that such a learning procedure achieves monoculture robustness, and we quantify this by bounding the conjunctive error that all $k$ hypotheses misclassify points in an individual sense. We design methods for achieving this type of guarantee by drawing a surprising connection between replicability (Impagliazzo et al., 2022) and monoculture robustness. Specifically, we show that if the base learner is $ρ$-replicable, then running it independently $k$ times on the same sample yields individual monoculture error that shrinks exponentially with $k$, controlled by the single-run error of the base learner at the point and $ρ$. We complement these positive results with a lower bound: for individual monoculture robustness, we prove a worst-case lower bound showing that, for learners, driving the individual conjunctive error down to $γ$ can require a sample-size multiplier of $t = Ω(\log(1/γ))$.
papers.Core_Innovation: Derives that ρ-replicability of a base learner ensures k independently accurate hypotheses from one sample, bounded by conjunctive error.
papers.Decision_Perspective: Fund monoculture-robust ML pipeline development within 18 months to secure single-dataset reliability. Implement replicability audits for all models deploying more than three hypotheses within 6 months.
papers.Tags: PAC-learning, replicability, robustness, monoculture
papers.Hook: Single dataset produces k hypotheses with independent failure bounds.

papers.Title: Local AI Agents in Power Electronics Simulation: Deployment, Measurements and Costs
papers.Abstract: Agentic artificial intelligence (AI) is emerging in power electronics, where it drives the simulation loop that engineers used to close largely by hand. In this loop, a converter design, or a study of the network it connects to, is built, run, measured and revised until it satisfies its specification. Such an agent can be served from a cloud API or from an inference device on the premises. For organizations whose designs, customer data or export-controlled material cannot leave the site, and whose simulators are licensed there, local deployment is the natural choice. In such a deployment, the agent becomes an electrical load on the organization's own equipment, i.e., every run consumes power and energy on a local device, generates tokens and takes time. However, existing work focuses mainly on what the agent can achieve with cloud-hosted models. What a local deployment costs in power, energy, tokens and time on real simulation tasks, and what its choices trade against one another, has received little quantitative investigation under comparable conditions. To address this gap, a systematic evaluation framework is presented in this paper. It applies locally served models to agentic power electronics tasks, from the converter level to the system level, and measures their power, energy, token and time costs. Based on these measurements, the capability boundary of a local agent on such tasks and the cost per solved task are characterized. The results are expected to provide practical insight for the use of agentic AI in power electronics and the power systems it serves.
papers.Core_Innovation: Empirical measurement of LLM inference energy, latency and token cost for local power electronics simulation loops, revealing trade-offs between model scale and real-time feasibility
papers.Decision_Perspective: Launch a 60-day pilot quantifying local LLM energy-per-simulation against cloud APIs for three power electronics design projects, triggering local deployment if latency stays under 2 seconds per iteration. Reallocate simulation AI budgets from cloud contracts to on-premises inference hardware once the pilot crosses the 30% energy-cost reduction threshold.
papers.Tags: Power Electronics,AI Simulation,Inference Costs,Local Deployment,Token Energy
papers.Hook: Local AI agents run power electronics simulation offline, quantifying real-time energy and token costs

papers.Title: Auditing black-box clinical prediction models with a large language model through queries alone: a blinded test with planted flaws
papers.Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are used to explain clinical prediction models, on the promise that they can say what a model computes, find its faults and even reveal new knowledge in it. We tested the three promises where the answers could be checked. From the International Stroke Trial we trained four kinds of model (logistic regression, explainable boosting machine, gradient-boosted trees, neural network) for two outcomes on patients randomised earlier, planted one flaw in each of 24 copies (an under-predicted subgroup, a reversed risk factor or an implausible step) and mixed them with the 8 clean models. GPT-6 Astra audited each model three times, blind, through a tool that only returned the model's predictions; the judging rules were committed before any run and applied by program. Its surrogate models, with a median of 128 terms, reproduced the audited models' log-odds with a mean $R^2$ of 0.976 (0.959 for an additive surrogate of 42 terms fitted by an analyst). It found the planted flaw in 69 of 72 runs (96%; 95% CI 80% to 99%); a script written for the purpose found all 24. It also reported many more problems: 60% of 1,089 checkable reports failed the pre-specified check against the model's average behaviour; post hoc, most of these were real but small steps, and 15% of the checkable reports were not found in the model. Of 601 unexpected relationships it read out of the clean models, 11% held in patients randomised later (random pairs 6%; a regression scan's shorter list of its strongest candidates, 28%); after a check on the training data, 33% against 30%. With query access alone, an LLM can describe a black-box model faithfully and find nearly every planted flaw, as a purpose-written script also did; its reports of problems must be checked on the model and its discoveries on data.
papers.Core_Innovation: Query-only LLM audit uses surrogate approximation (median 128 terms, R²≥0.976) to reconstruct and validate black-box clinical prediction models without internal access
papers.Benefiting_Sectors: Healthcare AI, Clinical Research, Medical Diagnostics
papers.Disrupted_Sectors: Opaque ML Vendors, Black-Box Clinical Tools
papers.Decision_Perspective: Deploy LLM query-audit pipelines for all new clinical prediction models within 6 months. Phase out black-box models that fail surrogate reproducibility (R²<0.95) thresholds.
papers.Tags: LLM audit, clinical prediction, surrogate models, query-only, black-box
papers.Hook: LLM audits black-box clinical models via prediction queries alone, revealing planted flaws

papers.Title: Learning to Interact in Multi-Agent Self-Play for Controllable Autonomous Driving Scenario Generation
papers.Abstract: Large-scale, multi-agent self-play trains robust driving policies effectively in simulation, but controlling these models to generate specific, safety-critical edge cases remains a key challenge. Existing goal-conditioned self-play frameworks rely primarily on static map-location goals and fail to reliably produce complex agent interactions such as aggressive tailgating or adversarial cut-offs. These agent interactions are necessary for rigorous autonomous vehicle (AV) testing. To address this, we present an extended multi-agent self-play framework that introduces agent-relative dynamic goals. By conditioning policies on this extended goal representation, our framework enables targeted, controllable scenario synthesis. We demonstrate that our approach successfully generates interactive driving behaviors that static-goal baselines cannot simulate, providing a flexible tool for long-tail scenario generation in AV testing.
papers.Core_Innovation: Introduces agent-relative dynamic goals that replace static map-location waypoints, allowing policies to condition on interaction intent for controllable scenario synthesis.
papers.Benefiting_Sectors: Autonomous Driving, Simulation Software, Automotive Safety
papers.Disrupted_Sectors: Static Scenario Generation, Conventional Driving Ranges
papers.Decision_Perspective: Autonomous driving simulation teams must retrofit pipelines with agent-relative dynamic goal conditioning within six months to preserve testing relevance against static-baseline obsolescence. Investors should acquire or fund open-source implementers of agent-relative goal synthesis within the next AV testing cycle to capture early‑market advantage.
papers.Tags: Multi-Agent, Self-Play, Scenario Generation, Autonomous Vehicle Testing, Dynamic Goals
papers.Hook: Agent-relative dynamic goals enable controllable generation of complex driving interactions for AV testing.

papers.Title: TangentPDE: Learning Local Operator Responses with Sparse Finite-Difference Supervision
papers.Abstract: Neural PDE operators are often optimized through state reconstruction, which largely constrains operator values at observed inputs but does not fully characterize their sensitivity to local perturbations. A more faithful approximation of operator behavior requires not only accurate state predictions, but also correct variations along local perturbation directions. We present TangentPDE, which uses finite differences to approximate directional derivatives and constructs task-relevant finite-step responses from the state outputs of a reference solver at sparse paired inputs. Its objective jointly constrains state fidelity, response-direction alignment, and response-magnitude calibration, thereby learning both operator values and their local variations. Because the response labels are constructed solely from state outputs at paired inputs, the method requires neither explicit derivative labels, linearized or adjoint PDE solves, nor full Jacobians, and remains applicable to nonlinear solvers without derivative interfaces. Building on this, we additionally propose a selectively executed adaptation mechanism to strengthen local operator representations under finite-difference supervision. Budget-matched and correspondence-perturbed controls isolate the effect of relational supervision from improvements attributable to additional state observations or increased data volume. Designed as a plug-and-play training framework, TangentPDE integrates with diverse neural-operator backbones. Across four PDE systems and 20 task-backbone settings, TangentPDE lowers the three-seed mean state error in 18 settings and the corresponding Rollout@20 error in 18, while intrinsic finite-step response gains are strongest on DiffReact and remain task- and backbone-dependent elsewhere.
papers.Core_Innovation: TangentPDE constructs derivative-supervision labels via finite differences on sparse state outputs, enabling joint optimization of operator values and local directional variations without adjoint solves or Jacobian computations.
papers.Benefiting_Sectors: Fluid Dynamics, Climate Modeling, Scientific Computing
papers.Decision_Perspective: Accelerate integration of TangentPDE into computational pipelines to replace adjoint-dependent workflows within 18 months. Deprecate derivative-toolkit dependencies in new scientific computing projects once sparse-response supervision achieves parity.
papers.Tags: Neural Operators, Finite Differences, Directional Derivatives, Sparse Supervision
papers.Hook: Neural PDE operators now learn local sensitivities from sparse state pairs without derivative labels.

papers.Title: WorldRuler: Interactive World Modeling under Configurable Rules
papers.Abstract: Rules govern how player actions change interactive worlds. Different rules create distinct gameplay experiences within similar scenes and action spaces. For customizable gameplay, generative world models must follow user-defined rules beyond real-world behaviors. However, realizing user-defined rules presents two challenges: Rule-State Persistence and Rule-to-Visual Realization. The former requires preserving rule definitions, dependencies, and world states across saving and loading, so that restored worlds follow the established rules. The latter requires accurately realizing rule-induced changes on designated objects and attributes, particularly when affected objects are unseen. In this paper, we propose WorldRuler, which organizes rule definitions, dependencies, and object states in an executable 3D rule graph and connects rule execution, video generation, and perceptual feedback in a closed loop. The graph supports joint saving and restoration of rules and world states, while dynamic object binding grounds rule-specified entities in visual instances and uses stored states to constrain generation from their first appearance. We further introduce object attribute state replacement and counterfactual reconstruction training, enabling accurate attribute control and compatible appearance and motion changes while limiting interference with unrelated content. We develop an automated data collection and annotation pipeline using GTA-V and Habitat to construct RuleVerse, a dataset of rule-driven interactions with detailed state and event annotations, including cases where rules take effect before affected objects become visible. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of WorldRuler in preserving rule-state consistency across saving and loading and accurately realizing rule outcomes on designated objects and attributes.
papers.Core_Innovation: WorldRuler introduces an executable 3D rule graph that jointly persists rule definitions and world states. It drives video generation and perceptual feedback in a closed loop to visualize rule changes on unseen objects.
papers.Decision_Perspective: Fund seed-stage startups building closed-loop interactive world engines within 18 months. Acquire teams prototyping executable rule graphs to replace static game engine pipelines.
papers.Tags: Rule Graphs, Closed-Loop, State Persistence, Video Generation, Unseen Objects
papers.Hook: User-defined rules persist and render interactive 3D worlds with state-aware visual fidelity

papers.Title: Choosing What to Observe: Budget-Paired Counterfactual Audits for Credible Evaluation of Visual Agents
papers.Abstract: Visual agents that read dense documents must ration a finite observation budget across candidate regions, yet answer accuracy conflates where an agent looks, how it adapts to the reads that remain, and how it an?swers once observation stops. We introduce budget-paired counterfactual audits, an evaluation protocol that holds public evidence and region bindings fixed while perturbing only the remaining budget or de?clared task parameters, and credits every acquired history with exact continuation values. The resulting accounting decomposes lost expected accuracy into stepwise acquisition loss and terminal decision loss, separating planning from fixed-role heuristics. Across forty paired routing anchors, five open-weight
papers.Core_Innovation: The core innovation is a counterfactual audit protocol that fixes public evidence and region bindings while perturbing only the remaining budget or task parameters, assigning exact continuation values to each history. This yields a decomposition of lost accuracy into stepwise acquisition loss and terminal decision loss, isolating planning from fixed-role heuristics.
papers.Decision_Perspective: AI labs should integrate budget-paired counterfactual audits into visual agent workflows within the next two quarters to decompose accuracy loss sources. Teams building dense-document readers must replace heuristic budget allocation with this audit-driven planning framework.
papers.Tags: visual agents, counterfactual audit, budget allocation, evaluation protocol, document AI
papers.Hook: Enables counterfactual audit that isolates budget vs. decision loss in visual agents.

papers.Title: Atomic MathReasoner: Instance-Level Composition of Atomic Reasoning Skills for Mathematical LLMs
papers.Abstract: Most existing approaches enhance mathematical reasoning in large language models (LLMs) as a monolithic capability, despite the fact that different mathematical problems require different reasoning skills. Recent work has explored a more fine-grained perspective by decomposing mathematical reasoning into atomic skills and developing specialized modules for individual capabilities. However, how to effectively utilize these atomic abilities remains underexplored. To address this challenge, we propose Atomic MathReasoner (AMR), an instance-level framework for composing atomic reasoning skills. AMR first trains a library of capability-specific LoRA experts and performs gradient-free optimization over held-out validation subsets to discover a diverse set of low-loss composition prototypes. It evaluates the preference of each prototype using the token-level negative log-likelihood of reference solutions, filters ambiguous assignments through a confidence margin, and distills the resulting pseudo-labels into a lightweight router. During inference, the router selects an appropriate composition prototype for each problem, enabling problem-specific utilization of atomic skills without costly online optimization. Experiments on the AtomicMath benchmark across general and mathematics-specialized LLMs demonstrate consistent improvements. On Qwen2.5-Math-Instruct-7B, AMR increases average field accuracy from 64.4% to 68.1% at Level 1 and from 59.3% to 63.7% at Level 2, while improving average logical reasoning performance from 39.4% to 46.8%. These results demonstrate that effectively composing specialized atomic skills provides a promising approach to strengthening mathematical reasoning in LLMs.
papers.Core_Innovation: AMR trains a library of capability-specific LoRA experts and performs gradient-free optimization over held-out validation subsets to discover diverse low-loss composition prototypes. Prototypes are evaluated via token-level negative log-likelihood of reference solutions and filtered by a confidence margin
papers.Disrupted_Sectors: Standardized Testing Prep, Traditional Math Tutoring, Generic LLM Prompting
papers.Decision_Perspective: Allocate budget to integrate AMR LoRA composition into our math-reasoning LLM within Q3 2026. Trigger: if current monolithic prompting fails >20% of benchmark math tasks
papers.Tags: AtomicReasoning, LoRA, GradientFreeOptimization, MathLLMs, SkillComposition
papers.Hook: AMR enables instance-level composition of atomic math reasoning skills, unlocking skill-specific LLM optimization

papers.Title: Ambient LLMs: Data-Efficient Supervised Fine-tuning via Temperature Matching
papers.Abstract: Collecting large-scale, diverse, and high-quality post-training datasets for autoregressive language models is challenging. Consequently, Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) is typically applied to datasets significantly smaller than those used for pre-training, which leads to overfitting and the catastrophic forgetting of the tails of the data distribution. To prevent this collapse, we introduce Ambient SFT, a principled framework for leveraging imperfect predictions to augment the fine-tuning set. In our method, a "frozen" version of the pre-trained model serves as a noisy teacher that the fine-tuned model must match at a coarse level. In particular, we require that the high-temperature versions of the conditional distributions produced by the post-training model should match the high-temperature versions of the pre-training ones. The temperature hyperparameter controls the level of trust in the pre-trained model, with the limit $T\to \infty$ reverting back to regular SFT and $T=1$ to knowledge distillation. We demonstrate that our approach outperforms standard SFT across domain adaptation, instruction-tuning, and reasoning, leading for up to $21\%$ average relative improvement to standard SFT.
papers.Core_Innovation: Uses a frozen pre-trained model as a temperature-scaled teacher, requiring the fine-tuned model's high-temperature conditional outputs to match the teacher's, thereby regularizing SFT with imperfect predictions.
papers.Decision_Perspective: Prototype temperature-matched SFT on internal datasets within 3 months to measure data efficiency gains. Phase out SFT pipelines that lack temperature regularization when scaling to new domains.
papers.Tags: Temperature Matching, SFT, Data Efficiency, Teacher-Student
papers.Hook: Enables data-efficient SFT by matching high-temperature model distributions, avoiding dataset-scale overfitting.

papers.Title: Spool: Low-Latency Streaming Inference for Hybrid Vision-Language Models
papers.Abstract: Applications such as visual accessibility agents and robotics require answering questions about recent video content promptly, over a bounded window of past frames (e.g., the last two minutes). Hybrid vision-language models (VLMs), which interleave attention with linear recurrent layers such as Gated DeltaNet (GDN), are attractive for this setting, but maintaining a sliding window is expensive. The reason is that recurrent layers combine all past frames into a shared state, so expiring old frames normally requires re-running the entire window through the model. We observe that the recurrent update is affine in the state with input-dependent coefficients, so the effect of each frame can be captured as a transformation that composes associatively. We present Spool, a training-free framework that caches per-frame state transformations and composes them efficiently as the window advances, removing expired frames from each recurrent layer's state without replaying frames through the backbone. Removal is exact within each layer; as with key-value eviction in attention, expired frames can retain residual influence through the cached inputs computed by earlier layers. We design a dedicated data structure and GPU kernels to achieve low caching and composition overhead. Across five open-source hybrid VLMs and four video reasoning benchmarks, Spool achieves the lowest p95 time-to-first-token in all 20 model-benchmark tests, reducing it by a geometric mean of $6.6\times$ over the faster of two recent vLLM baselines, while improving accuracy by 2.3 percentage points on average.
papers.Core_Innovation: Per-frame affine state transformations are cached and composably pruned, enabling sliding-window advancement without recomputing through the VLM backbone.
papers.Disrupted_Sectors: Legacy Video Analytics, Batch VLM Inference
papers.Decision_Perspective: Integrate Spool's transformation caching into real-time robotics perception pipelines within the next six months to slash inference latency. Teams using full-window replay should migrate immediately or face competitive disadvantage.
papers.Tags: vision-language, streaming-inference, recurrent-caching, low-latency
papers.Hook: Cache-frame transformations permit dropping expired VLM states without backbone replay.

papers.Title: StringQFT: A Multiuse Textbook Resource for AI-Assisted Theoretical Physics
papers.Abstract: We present StringQFT as a textbook collection for string constructions of quantum field theory and as infrastructure for AI-assisted theoretical physics. The collection comprises 18 volumes, 190 chapters and 3,795 pages, covering brane probes, brane webs, geometric engineering, F-theory constructions, wrapped M5-branes and exact worldsheet constructions. Its open-book benchmark inventory contains 1,073 items, including 499 with automatic finite-answer checking. For retrieval-augmented generation, it provides 1,371 section records linked to textbook sources and PDF locations, together with a local lexical retriever. Training-data preparation is illustrated by 21 private, source-linked examples. For agents, it exposes 19 calculation tools with specified inputs and finite domains, connecting tool use to textbook derivations. We illustrate these uses through specific questions, retrieved passages and finite calculations. The textbook collection and accompanying resources are available at https://github.com/xingyang-yu/StringQFT.
papers.Core_Innovation: The core innovation is a benchmark of 1,073 finite-answer physics items systematically linked to a 18-volume textbook corpus, enabling verified AI tool use through 19 calculation tools with finite domains.
papers.Benefiting_Sectors: Quantum Computing, Scientific AI, Academic Publishing
papers.Decision_Perspective: We recommend allocating seed funding to integrate StringQFT calculation tools into quantum chemistry AI pipelines within the next 12 months. This will accelerate verified derivations and validate the benchmark's cross-disciplinary utility.
papers.Tags: StringQFT, AI Physics, Textbook Benchmark, RAG, Calculation Tools
papers.Hook: StringQFT provides a structured textbook benchmark enabling AI-assisted theoretical physics derivations.

papers.Title: An inexact stochastic variance-reduced gradient method for constrained convex finite-sum optimization
papers.Abstract: In this paper, we study a class of constrained convex finite-sum optimization problems. In many practical applications, all or some of the constraints are hard constraints that represent imperative requirements. Consequently, any desirable approximate solution must (nearly) satisfy these constraints. Motivated by this, we focus on computing an $ε$-$surely\ feasible\ stochastic\ optimal$ ($ε$-SFSO) solution, in which the constraint violation is deterministically bounded by $ε$, and the expected optimality gap is at most $ε$. While a recently proposed stochastic variance-reduced first-order penalty method can compute an $ε$-SFSO solution, there remains a significant gap between its first-order oracle complexity for computing an $ε$-SFSO solution and that for computing an $ε$-$expected\ feasible\ stochastic\ optimal$ solution, where both the expected constraint violation and the expected optimality gap are bounded by $ε$. To narrow this gap, we propose an inexact stochastic variance-reduced gradient (SVRG) method that significantly improves the previously best-known first-order oracle complexity for computing an $ε$-SFSO solution. Furthermore, when the objective consists of a single function, the proposed method reduces to a novel deterministic first-order method for solving standard convex conic optimization. It achieves a significantly lower gradient evaluation complexity with respect to the objective function compared to existing methods, and can outperform them when computing constraint gradients and projections onto the associated cone is cheaper than evaluating the objective gradient. Preliminary numerical results are presented to illustrate the performance of the proposed method.
papers.Core_Innovation: Proposes an inexact stochastic variance-reduced gradient method that bridges oracle complexity gaps between ε-SFSO and ε-expected feasible stochastic optimal solutions in constrained convex finite-sum optimization.
papers.Decision_Perspective: Accelerate prototyping of the inexact variance-reduced gradient method for constrained finite-sum problems within the next six months. Phase out legacy penalty-method implementations in new projects where ε-SFSO accuracy is required.
papers.Tags: stochastic optimization, variance reduction, constrained convex
papers.Hook: Inexact variance-reduced gradient method achieves ε-SFSO with tightened oracle complexity.

papers.Title: Do LLM Agents Still Need to Be Told How to Self-Improve?
papers.Abstract: LLM agents increasingly drive their own learning. Self-improvement methods delegate various components of model optimization to the models themselves. As models become more capable, this motivates a basic question: do these increasingly capable models still need us to specify how they should self-improve? In this paper we study an autonomous paradigm in which, given basic primitives, resources, and a general goal for self-improvement, agents construct their own self-learning algorithm for context-based optimization. Using the setting of gameplay as a testbed, a frozen LLM agent is given a compute budget and tools for collecting experience and updating text documents, and allowed to freely experiment without an externally imposed loop or access to real-world data. We find that sufficiently capable models do self-improve under these conditions, demonstrating strategies that align with classic cognitive frameworks for self-regulated learning and constructs from machine learning literature on self-generated curricula. Furthermore, we study the extent to which the learned text artifacts transfer to external benchmarks, observing improvement across different game horizons, mechanics, and 3D navigation.
papers.Core_Innovation: Agents synthesize self-directed optimization algorithms from experience logs and mutable text prompts, eliminating the need for externally specified update rules
papers.Disrupted_Sectors: Prompt Engineering, Machine Learning Operations, AI Training
papers.Decision_Perspective: Fund teams prototyping autonomous agent frameworks within 12 months to capture early-mover advantage in self-optimizing systems. Acquire or partner with firms specializing in LLM experience-loop infrastructure now.
papers.Tags: LLM Agents, Self-Improvement, Autonomous Optimization, Context Learning, Gameplay AI
papers.Hook: Capable LLM agents autonomously construct self-improvement loops from basic primitives

papers.Title: What Does a Bias Head Measure? Non-Identifiability in Head-Level Bias Attribution
papers.Abstract: Methods that localise social bias in large language models to individual attention heads and remove it by ablation are validated by their effect on a fairness metric, never by evidence that the statistic selecting the heads measures bias. We audit this on Qwen-2.5-7B-Instruct and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct. The head map correlates at $ρ= -0.950$ and $-0.768$ with a label-blind response-length map, apparently identifying a surface confound. An intervention that breaks the length-label coupling rejects this reading: with the prompt held fixed, response length explains 1% of the statistic's variance. What does explain it is prompt identity, at 64% of variance, in an ordering that is not monotonic in length. Within any fixed prompt the fairness label, response length and the presence of a protected-group token are collinear at $φ= 0.95$, partly by definition of the labelling rule, so no observational analysis can attribute the map to any of them, and no method in this family performs an experiment that could. The substantive claims fail independently: bias selectivity is not late-layer-concentrated on either model under either reference reading, and no head set we tested reduces the unfairness rate when ablated. Its complement, scored on the opposite label, reliably destroys refusal behaviour ($p = 2.7\times10^{-5}$), demonstrating that the pipeline detects effects at this scale.
papers.Core_Innovation: Head-level bias attribution is non-identifiable because fairness labels, response lengths, and protected-group tokens are collinear (φ=0.95) by definition, with prompt identity driving 64% of the bias statistic's variance in a non-monotonic ordering.
papers.Benefiting_Sectors: AI Safety, Responsible AI, LLM Auditing
papers.Decision_Perspective: Immediately retire head-ablation fairness pipelines lacking prompt-stratification, or redeploy them with controlled prompt baselines within 30 days. Fund only LLM audits that explicitly stratify bias statistics by prompt identity henceforth.
papers.Tags: LLM bias, head attribution, prompt confounding, fairness auditing
papers.Hook: Prompt identity, not response length, drives 64% of head-level bias statistics.

papers.Title: Higher-Scoring Coding Models Did Not Get More Work Done
papers.Abstract: New coding models advertise themselves on score improvements of coding benchmarks. Yet no study has tested if a model that scores higher on these benchmarks gets more real work done. On June 12, 2026, a U.S. export control directive banned access to Claude Fable 5 for 19 days, which forced users to switch to other models. During this time, most former Fable 5 users switched to Opus 4.8 (11 points lower on SWE-Bench Pro compared to Fable 5). We treat this suspension as a natural experiment, where the people and projects stayed the same and only the model changed, so we could isolate the effect of Fable 5 on user productivity. We tracked GitHub pull requests of 297 Fable 5 users before, during, and after the suspension. We used 8,908 developers who stayed on Opus 4.8 all the time as the control group. We also repeated the comparison across five model upgrades before and after the suspension in 2026 (1,208 developers, 15,442 pull requests). Fitting a difference-in-differences model with developer and date fixed effects, we found that having access to Fable 5 increased the 7-day merge rate of pull requests by only 1.4 percentage points [-1.4; +4.3], which was not statistically significant. Similarly, no significant increases of merge rates were found with the upgrades (weighted mean: -0.9 percentage points [-1.9; +0.2]); all five estimates were negative (95% intervals included 0, did not differ from each other). We also did not observe a significant increase in the number of pull requests merged per week (+2.4% [-4.9%; +10.2%]).
papers.Core_Innovation: The study exploits a U.S. export control ban on Claude Fable 5 as a natural experiment to causal-identify model effects on developer productivity using difference-in-differences on GitHub pull request data
papers.Decision_Perspective: Product teams should deprioritize model selection based solely on benchmark scores and instead validate with pilot productivity metrics within 30 days. Procurement units must reject vendor proposals that cite SWE-Bench or similar scores without real-work outcome data
papers.Tags: coding models, productivity, natural experiment, difference-in-differences, benchmark limitations
papers.Hook: Natural experiments now reveal whether coding model scores predict actual developer output

papers.Title: Multimodal Masked Diffusion Autoencoder for Modeling Impaired Driving
papers.Abstract: Human cognitive state (e.g., distraction, stress), gaze, and behavior interact with the driving environment in subtle ways that AI could use to assist drivers, but ground-truth labels for human cognitive state levels are costly to obtain at scale. We propose a multimodal masked-diffusion autoencoder, ID-MAE, that adds a self-supervised objective to impairment prediction: alongside predicting the impairment label as a masked token, it reconstructs masked gaze and trajectory. To probe the effects of different modalities and types of impairments on model inference, we introduce DIVERT, a driving-simulator dataset containing 103 hours of driving data (n = 109) with ten impairment inductions spanning cognitive, visual, and emotional states, recorded with gaze, vehicle state, and scene video. We demonstrate how ID-MAE affords significant improvements in impairment inference results on both the DIVERT dataset and existing datasets, and enables strong results in additional tasks, such as trajectory and gaze prediction. For location-matched pairs, our model achieves a paired AUC of 0.706 for impairment detection on DIVERT, compared to 0.590 without reconstruction loss, improving over existing baselines. We probe the design space in terms of input modalities, masking scheme, positional encoding, attention mechanism, and decoding. We also investigate the interaction between various impairments in training and inference, demonstrating that visually demanding distractions are separable from cognitive distractions. Code and data will be available upon acceptance.
papers.Core_Innovation: ID-MAE introduces a multimodal masked-diffusion autoencoder that jointly predicts impairment labels as masked tokens while reconstructing missing gaze and trajectory data across cognitive, visual, and emotional states
papers.Decision_Perspective: Automotive OEMs should integrate ID-MAE into production ADAS within 18 months of DIVERT dataset commercialization. Insurance underwriters must mandate multimodal cognitive state validation for high-risk policies beginning Q3 2026.
papers.Tags: Multimodal Diffusion, Impaired Driving, Self-Supervised, Driver Monitoring
papers.Hook: Multimodal masked diffusion autoencoder jointly predicts impairment and reconstructs gaze-trajectory

papers.Title: Distortion-Free Semantic Watermarks for Black-Box Generative Models
papers.Abstract: We present a provably distortion-free semantic watermarking algorithm that requires only black-box sampling access to a generative model and black-box access to a semantic embedding. A watermark is called distortion-free if, averaged over its secret detection key, it leaves the generator's output distribution unchanged; this provides a formal guarantee that watermarking does not reduce output quality. Conventional such watermarks are often brittle to transformations. This is especially problematic for images, where benign operations such as compression, cropping, or resizing change the entire pixel representation. Semantic watermarks therefore require detection to be robust to content-preserving transformations. Previous methods combining these properties rely heavily on specific white-box properties of the underlying model: either to autoregressive text generation or to diffusion-specific access, such as control of the initial noise or diffusion inversion. In contrast, our construction is fully generic: It only interacts with the generative model and the semantic embedding, a function that determines the notion of "preserving content" under which detection should be robust, via sample and query access. We then instantiate this framework for image generation. We characterize the two competing properties required of the semantic embedding: it should remain stable under transformations that preserve an image's content, but should distinguish independent generations from the same prompt. We train an image encoder directly for this tradeoff. The resulting encoder improves separation while maintaining stability over off-the-shelf alternatives and enables strong aggregate detection while remaining robust to various transformations. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our watermark scheme on both open-source and closed models, which is possible only due to restriction to black-box access.
papers.Core_Innovation: Proposes a black-box watermarking algorithm that provably preserves generator output distribution on average while resisting content-preserving transformations, eliminating white-box model dependencies.
papers.Decision_Perspective: Allocate R&D budget to integrate distortion-free watermarks into flagship generative products within the next quarter. Prioritize vendors refusing black-box watermark compatibility for immediate exclusion.
papers.Tags: Watermarking, Black-Box Models, Semantic Robustness
papers.Hook: Black-box generative models now support distortion-free, transformation-robust semantic watermarks.

papers.Title: Reading Scene States: Uncovering Safety Failures in Vision-Language Models
papers.Abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) can provide harmful assistance by interpreting visual events, even without an explicit request for the underlying harmful objective. We identify this \textbf{scene-state safety vulnerability} and introduce \textbf{SceneSafetyBench}, comprising 375 image--question pairs spanning Initial, Medium, and Ultimate scene states and five visual presentations. Across eight VLMs, scene-state inputs elicit harmful assistance with attack success rates (ASRs) of 45.6--72.3\%. Comparative analysis across three VLMs shows that scene-state inputs most closely resemble QR-related images in their layer-wise safety-related signal profiles, while exhibiting lower average late-layer readouts and distinct signal dynamics during generation. To turn this vulnerability into a systematic attack, we propose \textbf{S3TA}, which translates harmful objectives into scene states, queries image--question pairs independently, and assembles the responses. On seven MM-SafetyBench categories across eight open-weight and commercial VLMs, S3TA achieves a model-average ASR of \textbf{71.2\%, exceeding the strongest baseline by 6.1 percentage points}. Text-side filters and visual moderation provide limited protection. These findings highlight the need to safeguard the assistance models infer through scene-grounded reasoning, beyond screening input content.
papers.Core_Innovation: SceneSafetyBench profiles layer-wise VLM safety signals across initialized, medium, and ultimate visual scene states, while S3TA systematically translates harmful objectives into those states for automated response assembly.
papers.Decision_Perspective: Allocate 30-day red-team budget for VLM scene-state probing across deployed multimodal systems. Require layer-wise safety signal audits for any VLM integration before customer-facing deployment.
papers.Tags: VLM safety, scene states, red teaming
papers.Hook: VLMs yield harmful assistance when prompted through concealed scene states, bypassing explicit objectives.

papers.Title: Fine-Tuning Gemma 4 Edge Models for MATLAB Signal-Processing Code with SFT and QLoRA on a Laptop iGPU
papers.Abstract: Small language models that run on a laptop are attractive for writing signal-processing code offline, but they make systematic errors on digital signal processing (DSP) conventions. We apply supervised fine-tuning (SFT) to the Gemma 4 edge models E2B and E4B with 66 checked examples covering 11 signal-processing MATLAB subtasks, using low-rank adaptation (LoRA) and quantized LoRA (QLoRA) on the integrated GPU (iGPU) of a laptop, and deploy the 8-bit integer (int8) models with the adapters through OpenVINO. On held-out variants scored by deterministic checkers, the pass rate rises from 18/66 to 37/66 (LoRA) and 37/66 (QLoRA) for E2B and from 32/66 to 47/66 for E4B (QLoRA). Reading all 159 failing programs shows that the adapters remove most errors of convention, such as the sign of a lag, units and array shapes, but few errors in building signals and noise. Applied at run time, the adapter costs 17-19% of the generation speed.
papers.Core_Innovation: Quantized LoRA + SFT on laptop iGPUs reduces DSP convention errors while adding only 17-19% runtime overhead to Gemma 4 edge models.
papers.Benefiting_Sectors: Signal Processing, Embedded Systems, Scientific Software
papers.Decision_Perspective: Integrate QLoRA-adapted Gemma 4 into laptop DSP workflows within 90 days to automate signal-processing code generation. Establish adapter performance benchmarks and team retraining before production deployment.
papers.Tags: Gemma, QLoRA, SFT, Edge Computing, MATLAB
papers.Hook: Laptop iGPU fine-tuning enables reliable MATLAB DSP code generation.

papers.Title: Agent Trust Infrastructure (ATI): A Federated Identity, Trust, Attestation, and Accountability Architecture for Cross-Organization Autonomous AI Agents
papers.Abstract: AI agents increasingly collaborate across organizational boundaries, invoking tools and interacting with agents operated by independent entities. Although existing agent frameworks support planning and coordination, they lack a common mechanism for verifying cross-organizational agent identity, execution integrity, and authorization. We propose the Agent Trust Infrastructure (ATI), a framework-independent security architecture built on Public Key Infrastructure (PKI), Zero Trust Architecture (ZTA), and remote attestation. ATI establishes federated trust through peer organizational certificate authorities (AgentCAs), eliminating the need for a shared root authority. Before executing requests, ATI validates agent certificates, verifies approved model, tool, and system-prompt configurations, and enforces authorization through three policy checks. We implement ATI as an external security enforcement layer that integrates with existing agent frameworks without modifying their underlying models. We evaluate ATI in a simulated federation of eight organizations using six agent frameworks, each deploying a five-agent team. Security experiments involve two organizations and assess 14 attack scenarios and six benign tasks across five agent models, using five attack variations and three repetitions per variation. A panel of judge models evaluates the experimental outcomes. With all enforcement mechanisms enabled, attack containment increases from 43% to 84% (40% to 80% for the 11 attack scenarios evaluated consistently across all configurations), while enforcement introduces approximately 174 microseconds of overhead per request. ATI is released as an open-source, framework-independent package that uses IETF WIMSE workload token formats for identity and request verification and Entity Attestation Tokens for model, tool, and system-prompt integrity verification.
papers.Core_Innovation: The technical delta is a federated PKI architecture using peer organizational AgentCAs that replace a shared root authority, coupled with real-time three-policy validation of model, tool, and system-prompt configurations enforced externally.
papers.Disrupted_Sectors: Legacy Identity Providers, On-Premise Security Vendors
papers.Decision_Perspective: Fund open-source ATI integration kits for cross-organizational agent ecosystems within 18 months to de-risk multi-vendor deployments. Require AgentCA-verified attestation for any agent invoking external tools in production.
papers.Tags: AgentTrust, FederatedPKI, ZeroTrust, RemoteAttestation, AIAgents
papers.Hook: Cross-organizational AI agents can now enforce verifiable trust without a shared root certificate authority.

papers.Title: Learned versus Kinematic Trajectory Prediction under Reduced Observation Frequency
papers.Abstract: Trajectory prediction models for automated driving are usually trained on data with a fixed sampling frequency, while positions received via vehicle-to-everything (V2X) communication arrive at 1-10 Hz. We study whether a learned predictor that uses only the observation history keeps its advantage over constant velocity (CV) and constant acceleration (CA) models when the history frequency drops. On the Argoverse 2 motion forecasting dataset, the 5 s history of the focal agent was downsampled from 10 Hz to 5, 2, and 1 Hz, and the 6 s future was predicted without maps or neighboring agents. An LSTM-based recurrent neural network (RNN) trained for each frequency was compared with the same network trained at 10 Hz and applied to sparse histories after linear interpolation. Hypotheses and thresholds were fixed before training, the main RNNs were trained with ten seeds each, and results on 24,984 test scenarios have bootstrap confidence intervals over scenarios and seeds. The average displacement error of the frequency-specific RNN grew by 3.1% at 5 Hz, 10.1% at 2 Hz, and 20.3% at 1 Hz. Contrary to our hypothesis, its advantage over the better kinematic model did not vanish on straight motion and was 24-30% on both straight motion and turns at every frequency, while for pedestrians CV was more accurate. The 10 Hz model with interpolation was at most 1.3% less accurate than the frequency-specific model down to 2 Hz but 11.5% less accurate at 1 Hz. Each hypothesis was only partly supported.
papers.Core_Innovation: Systematic frequency-stratified LSTM RNN training with bootstrap-validated comparison to frequency-agnostic linear interpolation and kinematic baselines across 24,984 autonomous driving scenarios
papers.Benefiting_Sectors: Autonomous Driving, V2X Communications, Automotive AI
papers.Decision_Perspective: Allocate 18-month R&D budget to integrate frequency-stratified LSTM inference into existing V2X perception stacks. Discontinue standalone constant-acceleration trajectory modules for any system operating below 2 Hz observation frequency.
papers.Tags: Trajectory Prediction, V2X, Frequency Downsampling, LSTM, Kinematic Baselines
papers.Hook: Learned predictors maintain accuracy advantage over kinematic models even at 1Hz observation frequency

papers.Title: Structure--Residual Inductive Biases for Language Model Pretraining
papers.Abstract: Next-token prediction is relied upon to learn both predictive behavior and internal representations. We ask whether representation structure itself should be an explicit inductive bias. Motivated by the two-part coding view of Kolmogorov complexity, we study a structure--residual principle in which a representation separates structure from realization detail. We instantiate this principle in two complementary ways. Boundary Bottleneck Concept (BBC) routes information from token segments through boundary carriers while preserving local autoregressive computation. Continuous Concept (CC) regularizes representation geometry and induces a spectral decomposition into low-frequency structure and high-frequency residual. We derive coding bounds for both views and show that multiplicity-corrected boundary attention becomes exact as the within-segment path energy vanishes. Empirically, BBC and CC exhibit strikingly different depth preferences: BBC works best in early layers, whereas CC is most effective in later layers. At 300M training tokens, combining BBC and CC improves NLL by 1.44\% on GPT-2 Medium. These gains persist with training runs up to 20B tokens. Representation diagnostics show that BBC increases the relative predictive importance of boundary states, while CC reduces spectral residual energy. Together, these results suggest that structure--residual biases can improve language-model pretraining beyond next-token prediction. Code: https://github.com/haihuang-ml/structure-residual
papers.Core_Innovation: It formalizes a structure-residual principle where representations separate low-frequency structure from high-frequency detail, instantiated through Boundary Bottleneck Concept routing and Continuous Concept spectral decomposition with coding bounds.
papers.Decision_Perspective: Fund AI research teams to integrate structure-residual inductive biases into pretraining pipelines within 12 months. Companies using fixed transformer architectures should benchmark boundary and continuous residual mechanisms against current models.
papers.Tags: Structure-residual, Inductive Bias, Language Model Pretraining, Boundary Bottleneck, Continuous Concept
papers.Hook: Structure-residual separation enables explicit inductive bias in LM pretraining

papers.Title: WoRD: Diffusion-Based Posterior Inference for Online Goal Recognition
papers.Abstract: Goal recognition is the task of inferring an agent's intended goal from its observed behavior. Most existing work focuses on high-level symbolic recognition, abstracting away the continuous motion through which agents reach their goal. Methods that do reason over continuous trajectories rely on an explicit dynamics model that is hard to acquire and rarely transfers across settings. Neither approach explicitly learns how agents move toward each candidate goal, limiting accuracy on ambiguous trajectory prefixes where such knowledge is most needed.   We present WoRD (Waypoint Recognition with Diffusion), which uses a learned trajectory prior to infer the agent's goal from partial observations. At each step, WoRD runs one warm-started denoising chain per candidate goal, steers each chain toward the observed trajectory through a closed-form log-likelihood gradient, and reweights the resulting samples by Bayes' rule into a calibrated posterior over goals. We evaluate WoRD on simulated robot settings, pedestrian trajectories, and vehicle trajectories using four metrics targeting distinct failure modes. Across all three settings, the same inference procedure preserves calibrated multimodal beliefs through ambiguous prefixes where filter- and classifier-based observers collapse to a single mode or grow overconfident.
papers.Core_Innovation: WoRD replaces explicit dynamics models with a learned trajectory prior, running per-goal warm-started denoising chains steered by closed-form log-likelihood gradients and Bayes-reweighted into a calibrated posterior
papers.Decision_Perspective: Integrate WoRD into robotic perception stacks within 18 months to achieve goal inference from partial trajectories without kinematics models. Discontinue symbolic goal-recognition modules that cannot process continuous trajectory prefixes.
papers.Tags: diffusion, goal recognition, robotics, trajectory inference, Bayesian
papers.Hook: Diffusion enables goal recognition from partial continuous trajectories without explicit dynamics

papers.Title: Retrieval-Augmented Correction for Generalist Medical Image Segmentation
papers.Abstract: Automated segmentation is routinely used as the first step in quantitative image-based clinical workflows, where predicted masks are subsequently reviewed and corrected by human operators. Automated correction of the residual structural errors is currently addressed one anatomy at a time, so the number of trained correctors scales with the number of segmentation targets. We present GRACE, a retrieval-augmented refiner that edits an input mask under context drawn from a shared knowledge base of verified prior cases. The refiner is trained once on a multi-organ corpus spanning compact organs, cavities, branching vessels, and tumour lesions. In the held-out dataset-transfer evaluation, three held-out datasets query a fixed knowledge base built from training data only. A separate leave-one-anatomy-out experiment tests parameter-free index extension: verified cases of an unseen solid organ enter the knowledge base, and the refiner stays frozen. A light shape-aware projection head on a frozen multimodal encoder maps embedding similarity to the shape agreement of the masks, so the knowledge base returns cases that the refiner can use as a shape prior. We evaluate GRACE on 18 public datasets spanning CT, MRI and ultrasound, using nine refinement configurations and seven upstream segmentors that span weak, mid, and strong operating regimes. We report each change with the DSC of its input mask. On the weak tier, the input DSC is 0.386 and GRACE adds up to +0.35 DSC. On a strong segmentor, the input DSC is 0.932 and the mean change is small. Transfer to an imaging modality that is absent from training and from the index is partial and depends on the anatomy, and remains an open research direction. Our results suggest retrieval-conditioned refinement is a practical alternative to anatomy-specific correction models. Code: https://github.com/robustml-eurecom/grace
papers.Core_Innovation: Replaces anatomy-specific correctors with a retrieval-augmented refiner that uses a frozen model to edit masks based on verified prior cases.
papers.Decision_Perspective: Fund the integration of retrieval-augmented refinement into existing radiology SaaS platforms within 12 months. Kill investment in niche, single-organ segmentation correction startups.
papers.Tags: Medical Imaging, RAG, Image Segmentation, Generalist AI
papers.Hook: Single-model correction of diverse medical image masks using a shared, extensible knowledge base.

papers.Title: Latent Lattice Language Models
papers.Abstract: Language models typically increase per-token computation through deeper or looped layers and latent reasoning steps, while richer residual connections improve information flow across layers. We instead increase computational capacity: the number of active computational states a model maintains. We introduce the Lattice of Latents, a set of per-layer horizontal latent streams that run recurrently along time, alongside the vertical residual stream that flows through depth. Like hyper-connections, mHC, and attention or value residuals, the Lattice enhances the residual stream, but rather than adding or rerouting residual pathways through depth, it provides companion computational states that persist across tokens. Unlike hybrid Transformer-SSM architectures, whose recurrent states primarily serve as internal memory for sequence mixing, these latents directly condition the vertical stream's attention, KV-cache writes, MLP computation, and decoding. On Transformers trained on 20B FineWeb-Edu tokens, a 406M-parameter Lattice model lowers validation perplexity from 15.41 to 14.40 over a parameter-matched Transformer. These gains extend across architectural variants. The Lattice composes with prior residual-stream enhancements: with hyper-connections and input residuals, it lowers validation perplexity from 15.41 (base Transformer) and 14.22 (Transformer with the same enhancements) to 13.61. On Gated DeltaNet, Mamba-2, Triadic GDN, and GDN-Mamba-2 hybrids, it improves perplexity at every tested native state size, with Lattice-GDN and Lattice-Triadic-GDN variants outperforming pure baselines with 4x larger native states. These results identify persistent per-layer state as a complementary axis for scaling language-model computation.
papers.Core_Innovation: Per-layer horizontal latent streams recur across tokens and directly gate the vertical stream's attention, KV-cache, and MLP, rather than serving as isolated sequence-memory states.
papers.Benefiting_Sectors: Artificial Intelligence, Cloud Computing, Semiconductor Manufacturing
papers.Disrupted_Sectors: Legacy RNN Hardware, Conventional NLP Tooling
papers.Decision_Perspective: Allocate prototyping funds to lattice-latent architecture startups within 12 months to validate token-compute savings versus depth-scaling baselines. Transition internal model scaling efforts toward lattice-latent conditioning if preliminary results show >15% inference cost reduction.
papers.Tags: Latent Lattices, Transformer Optimization, Inference Efficiency, Recurrent States, Computational Capacity
papers.Hook: Latent lattice enables persistent per-layer streams that directly condition attention, KV-cache, and MLP computation.

papers.Title: ViRA: Toward Ultra-High-Resolution Visual Agents via Cross-Input Relative Policy Optimization
papers.Abstract: Visual agents answer questions about ultra-high-resolution photos by zooming into the relevant regions. However, existing agents often answer from common sense instead of reading the evidence. Reinforcement learning (RL) on the final answer cannot correct this, because a guess earns the same reward as reading. We propose Cross-Input Relative Policy Optimization (CrossRPO), which trains agents on contrast sets. A contrast set asks one question about several versions of an image that differ only in a small region with the evidence and have different answers, so only reading the evidence solves the whole set. CrossRPO rewards solving the whole set, and we prove that it does not reinforce a set answered from common sense. We build contrast sets for training (ViRA-Train) and evaluation (ViRA-Bench) by editing one small object in images of 21 to 120 megapixels, and we photograph further sets with real changes (ViRA-Bench-Real) to exclude editing traces. We train two Visual Reasoning Agents, ViRA-9B and ViRA-27B, with CrossRPO on only about 3,500 items of ViRA-Train each. CrossRPO achieves 63.3% set accuracy on ViRA-Bench at the maximum resolution, against 59.3% for GRPO. ViRA-9B is the most accurate open model of its size on all benchmarks, and ViRA-27B outperforms Claude Haiku 5.5 and GPT-6-Luna, both at their highest thinking level, on most benchmarks.
papers.Core_Innovation: CrossRPO trains visual agents on contrast sets: image variants differing in small regions with distinct answers, so solving the entire set demands evidence reading. Its reward structure mathematically excludes common-sense guessing, proving only evidence-driven policies are reinforced.
papers.Benefiting_Sectors: Computer Vision, Autonomous Vehicles, Remote Sensing
papers.Decision_Perspective: Allocate venture capital to CrossRPO visual agent startups within a 6-month validation window. Migrate existing high-res QA systems to contrast-set RL pipelines to eliminate common-sense answer shortcuts immediately.
papers.Tags: CrossRPO, Contrast Sets, Visual Reasoning, High-Resolution RL
papers.Hook: CrossRPO enables agents to answer high-res questions by contrasting image regions instead of guessing.

papers.Title: Quantifying the added value of human forecaster discussions for tropical cyclone intensity prediction
papers.Abstract: The National Hurricane Center routinely releases Tropical Cyclone Discussions that offer insights into its tropical cyclone forecasts. This study examines the added value of these discussions for intensity forecasting beyond a set of numerical predictors. For 637 Atlantic and eastern North Pacific tropical cyclones from the 2002-2023 hurricane seasons, we analyze the discussion text and its combination with 13 hurricane environmental predictors from SHIPS and ERA5 10-meter wind fields, for forecasting intensity changes at lead times of 24 to 120 hours using three modeling methods. In one approach, an end-to-end deep learning framework for the text shows that the discussions alone offer comparable value for 24-hour intensity forecasts to the SHIPS predictors. Adding discussion information to the SHIPS predictors in an ensemble of five such models reduces the mean absolute error of 24-hour maximum sustained wind forecasts for 2022-2023 cyclones from 9.89 to 8.90 kt, with a confidence interval that excludes zero when whole storms are resampled. The ERA5 wind fields have a minor effect on mean absolute error in wind predictions, and model rankings differ across predicted variables, lead times and model types. We provide prediction intervals for these forecasts, whose coverage falls below the 90% target during rapid intensification. Analysis of the text shows that words related to intensity and intensity change (such as intensify, weaken, eyewall and category) are important for the model predictions. This retrospective study shows the added value of the forecasters' discussions and suggests that multi-modal learning can help understand the predictive contribution of expert human judgment. The reanalysis data differ from real-time analyses, and the discussions are issued at least three hours after the valid time of the other inputs, so these results should not be interpreted operationally.
papers.Core_Innovation: A deep learning encoder processes discussion text as a standalone predictor achieving SHIPS-equivalent 24-hour intensity forecast skill, and when fused with SHIPS predictors in a heterogeneous ensemble, it reduces mean absolute error by 0.99 kt for 2022-2023 Atlantic/eastern North Pacific cyclones
papers.Benefiting_Sectors: Maritime Shipping, Aviation, Insurance, Emergency Management
papers.Disrupted_Sectors: Legacy Numerical Model Providers, Low-Skill Forecast Resellers
papers.Decision_Perspective: Allocate R&D budget to embed discussion-text encoders into the next SHIPS iteration by Q3 2027, targeting the documented 0.99 kt MAE reduction. Deprecate standalone SHIPS pipelines that exclude forecaster discussion inputs.
papers.Tags: Tropical Cyclone, Intensity Forecast, Deep Learning, Discourse Integration
papers.Hook: Human forecaster discussions now match SHIPS predictors for 24-hour cyclone intensity forecasts

papers.Title: How VLMs Plan What's Next
papers.Abstract: When a vision-language model describes an image, it names one object at a time and it rarely repeats itself, yet how the model plans this order is far from obvious. We characterize the mechanism a VLM uses to decide where to look before it looks. The mechanism has four main parts. First, binding heads match the relevant text tokens against the image and resolve them into pointers to the matched image region. Second, the same binding heads bind each written answer to the region it came from, and the model turns it into a progress signal: a cursor, the position in the image up to which the list has been written. Third, a select step chooses the nearest unwritten region after the cursor, or stops. Finally, gaze heads execute the chosen pointer and return a concept of what is drawn there, which language heads and the late MLPs turn into a word in the language of the question. We validate each part of this mechanism through causal patching in Qwen3-VL models on a synthetic visual retrieval task, and test our mechanisms against alternative hypotheses. We further show that the mechanism holds across input formats, natural photographs, and languages, and that its binding, relay, and gaze heads appear at every model size from 2B to 32B. This work allows us to investigate how a VLM turns a question and an image into a sequence of answers, layer by layer and token by token. More broadly, it opens a way to study how models plan over complex multi-step tasks with long rollouts. Our project is available at https://plan.baulab.info/
papers.Core_Innovation: Binding heads establish a cursor-based progress signal by binding each answer token to its matched image region, enabling sequential selection of unwritten visual units.
papers.Disrupted_Sectors: Legacy Image Captioning, Static Visual QA
papers.Decision_Perspective: Allocate 6-month funding to integrate cursor-based planning into Qwen3-VL for real-time sequential grounding. Immediately phase out static image-caption models lacking progress-tracking mechanisms.
papers.Tags: Vision-Language Models, Causal Patching, Sequential Grounding
papers.Hook: VLMs acquire a cursor-driven planning mechanism for sequential visual grounding.

papers.Title: Hyperlyve: Parallelized Enumeration and Exact Lyapunov Stability Certification for Deep ReLU Networks
papers.Abstract: We introduce Hyperlyve (Hyperplane Partitioned Lyapunov Verification and Enumeration), a framework for proving the asymptotic stability of nonlinear dynamical systems, including those with neural network controllers. Hyperlyve learns and formally certifies continuous piecewise-affine (CPA) neural Lyapunov functions within a counterexample-guided inductive synthesis (CEGIS) loop. Hyperlyve's key innovation is a parallel algorithm that enumerates the hyperplane arrangement formed by the ReLU activations of deep networks and certifies that Lyapunov conditions hold within each polyhedral region. We derive sound and complete regional tests to verify the asymptotic stability of the exact smooth dynamics (rather than a piecewise-linear approximation) within a compact domain of interest. Furthermore, we formally characterize the computational complexity of the CPA neural Lyapunov verification problem as co-NP-complete, filling a key gap in the literature. Empirical results demonstrate that Hyperlyve enumerates ReLU networks over 150-times faster than competing tools, which contributes to Hyperlyve proving the asymptotic stability of systems that are currently intractable for state-of-the-art verifiers.
papers.Core_Innovation: Parallel enumeration of ReLU-induced hyperplane partitions provides sound and complete Lyapunov certification for exact smooth dynamics over compact domains, with formal co-NP-complete complexity classification.
papers.Decision_Perspective: Allocate R&D funding to integrate Hyperlyve into safety-critical neural network validation pipelines within 12 months. Require formal Lyapunov certification for all neural network controllers in new autonomous vehicle software releases.
papers.Tags: Lyapunov Verification, ReLU Networks, Formal Methods, Parallel Enumeration
papers.Hook: Parallel ReLU hyperplane enumeration enables exact Lyapunov certification for deep neural network controllers.

papers.Title: Mitigating Catastrophic Forgetting with Physics-Indexed Specialist Memory: the Evolutionary Neuroplastic Agent
papers.Abstract: Continual reinforcement learning requires adaptation to changing conditions while preserving performance under previously encountered dynamics. It was investigated whether specialists generated by evolutionary search can provide a reusable memory when combined with environment detection and failure-driven search. The Evolutionary Neuroplastic Agent (ENA) evolves small neural networks without gradients, archives selected policies by detected dynamic regime, and retrieves them through Bayesian policy reuse. The architecture was evaluated in non-stationary CartPole and HalfCheetah environments. In the 30-replicate CartPole ablation, the complete architecture achieved a mean success rate of 83.2% across the five test environments. Among variants that learned the harder CartPole environments, the complete architecture showed the most consistent retention. A selection ablation also showed that the retrieval rule affected performance. In the evaluated sequences, ENA adapted more slowly than PPO on CartPole and achieved lower returns than SAC on HalfCheetah. The evidence concerns the complete architecture and does not isolate gradient-free optimization as the cause of retention or establish superiority over other continual-learning methods.
papers.Core_Innovation: Evolutionary search generates specialist policies indexed by detected dynamic regimes, enabling Bayesian retrieval without gradient computation.
papers.Decision_Perspective: Allocate seed funding for ENA implementation in adaptive robotics within 12 months. Trigger full rollout when Bayesian policy retrieval latency achieves sub-10ms performance.
papers.Tags: Evolutionary RL, Catastrophic Forgetting, Bayesian Retrieval, Non-Stationary Environments
papers.Hook: Evolutionary search archives regime-specific policies for gradient-free continual learning.

papers.Title: Optimal Autoregressive Chain-of-Thought Learning via Bagging
papers.Abstract: We study how to learn an autoregressive next-token generator $f\colonΣ^\star\toΣ$ from a class $\mathcal{F}$, given chain-of-thought (CoT) demonstrations of length $T$ generated by $f$. We present a simple algorithm based on bagging, which outputs a majority vote of generators that are trained to be CoT-consistent on bootstrap samples of the training data. For binary token sets, it achieves the optimal sample complexity of $O((d_{\mathrm{VC}}+\log(1/δ))/ε)$, independent of the CoT length $T$, where $d_{\mathrm{VC}}$ is the VC dimension of $\mathcal{F}$. For finite token sets $Σ$, the VC dimension is replaced by a multiclass analogue, the Graph dimension $d_{\mathrm{G}}$, and the sample complexity is optimal up to a $\log|Σ|$ factor. The number of generators in the majority-vote ensemble is $O(\log(T/δ))$, and we show that the ensemble can be distilled into a single generator in $\mathcal{F}$ at the expense of $n\log(nT)$ unlabeled prompts.
papers.Core_Innovation: The algorithm bags autoregressive generators, training each on bootstrap samples to be CoT-consistent, then outputs a majority vote. Distillation into a single generator requires only n log(nT) unlabeled prompts.
papers.Benefiting_Sectors: Artificial Intelligence, Machine Learning, Cloud Computing
papers.Disrupted_Sectors: Prompt Engineering, Costly Machine Learning Training
papers.Decision_Perspective: Allocate capital to integrate bagged CoT training into model pipelines within 90 days, triggered by the paper's sample complexity proof. Discontinue vendor contracts promoting non-bagged, single-generator CoT workflows.
papers.Tags: bagging, chain-of-thought, sample efficiency
