papers.Hook: Bagged CoT learners achieve optimal sample complexity independent of reasoning length.

papers.Title: SADL: On the Demand-Supply Geometry of Representation Collapse
papers.Abstract: In Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPAs), a well-constrained projector output does not by itself prevent representation collapse. We find that, from initialization, the encoder representation is dominated by a component shared by different inputs. A batch-normalized projector removes this component, so regularization after the projector cannot correct it, and the differences between representations shrink until they collapse. We propose SADL (Supply And Demand Loss), which keeps the original training objective and constrains the encoder directly when needed. SADL compares the representation differences that the projector output demands with the differences the encoder can retain and pass on to the projector, and adds a constraint on the encoder only when supply falls short of demand. It works with different Demand Regularizers and introduces no auxiliary networks, additional trainable parameters, or architectural changes. In single-task and jointly trained four-task LeWorldModel (LeWM) and INTACT experiments, SADL lowers the collapse rate over ten random seeds from 50% to 0%. After one epoch of training, encoder effective rank is 3.4-6.4 times that of the corresponding baseline without SADL, and latent prediction error falls to 1/20-1/303 of it. Without additional tuning, SADL stays robust as its loss weight spans orders of magnitude, and with several Demand Regularizers INTACT exceeds 95% mean search-free control success. On four image datasets, SADL also consistently improves accuracy and stability across random seeds. These results show that matching the representation differences a regularizer demands with the differences the encoder can supply leads to faster and more stable representation learning in control and image classification.
papers.Core_Innovation: SADL inserts a supply-demand gap check directly onto the encoder, adding regularization only when encoder representation differences cannot meet the projector's demanded differences, preserving discriminative detail without extra parameters or architectural overhaul
papers.Benefiting_Sectors: Computer Vision, Autonomous Driving, Robotics Simulation
papers.Decision_Perspective: Mandate SADL integration into all active JEPAs within 90 days to lock in representation diversity. Immediately deprioritize projector-only regularization pipelines that cannot satisfy the supply-demand constraint trigger.
papers.Tags: JEPAs, representation collapse, supply-demand loss, self-supervised learning, encoder regularization
papers.Hook: Enables JEPAs to prevent representation collapse by directly constraining encoder supply against projector demand without auxiliary parameters

papers.Title: Surrogate-Assisted Compact-Model Extraction for SKY130 CMOS at 77 K
papers.Abstract: Cryogenic circuit design requires compact transistor models that reproduce measured low-temperature behavior and run in standard circuit simulators. We fit BSIM4 parameters to measured I-V curves of SkyWater 130 nm (SKY130) transistors at 77 K using a neural surrogate of NGSpice. The surrogate maps compact-model parameters and device geometry to the complete set of output and transfer characteristics. Extraction is a bounded least-squares search: a bank of NGSpice simulations supplies initial candidates, finite differences of the surrogate supply the local Jacobian, and NGSpice re-simulates the resulting cards before selection. On 18 measured geometries, we compare a search over seven card parameters with a search over 43 parameters selected by NGSpice sensitivity. Relative to NGSpice re-simulations of the previously released cards, the two searches reduce the in-sample mean relative root-mean-square error (RRMS) by 17% and 26%, respectively. The 43-parameter search has the lower overall error, but the seven-parameter search has the lower mean on high-bias curves, and some individual curves have higher error than with the released cards under both searches.
papers.Core_Innovation: A neural surrogate of NGSpice approximates output and transfer characteristics, enabling bounded least-squares BSIM4 parameter extraction at 77 K without full simulations at every iteration.
papers.Benefiting_Sectors: Cryogenic Electronics, Space Electronics, Quantum Computing
papers.Decision_Perspective: Integrate this surrogate-assisted extraction pipeline into cryogenic IP platforms within 12 months. Partner with SKY130 foundries to validate models at 77 K for quantum computing workloads.
papers.Tags: Cryogenic,BSIM4,Neural Surrogate,Compact Model Extraction,SKY130
papers.Hook: Neural surrogate enables cryogenic BSIM4 parameter extraction for SKY130 transistors in standard simulators.

papers.Title: CertiSum: Bitwise-Identical MXFP4 Training Across Platforms and Parallelism Layouts
papers.Abstract: Training with MXFP4, a 4-bit microscaling format, is non-deterministic: identical inputs can produce different results across parallelism layouts and GPU vendors. These differences complicate debugging and training audits and can cause training and inference engines to disagree. We present CertiSum to make MXFP4 training bitwise invariant across runs, parallelism layouts, and GPU vendors. Its key insight is that native FP32 accumulation of MXFP4 products is often already exact for every summation order. CertiSum collects statistics during quantization to certify native matrix multiplication results, recomputes uncertified outputs exactly, and uses exact kernels directly where certification rarely succeeds. CertiSum keeps quantization blocks unchanged across layouts and merges partial sums without rounding, including in attention and weight-gradient computation. In 200-step Qwen3-8B-Base experiments, CertiSum preserves training states bit for bit across AMD MI350X and NVIDIA GB200 and across changes in data, tensor, and context parallelism on MI350X. Across three 8B--14B models on FineWeb-Edu using MI350X, it adds 11.8--60.5% to training-step latency relative to its non-exact MXFP4 counterpart at the larger evaluated input shapes, with speedups of up to $1.24\times$ over BF16 and $1.70\times$ over deterministic BF16.
papers.Core_Innovation: CertiSum exploits the fact that FP32 accumulation of MXFP4 products is often exact, then certifies matrix multiplication results during quantization and merges partial sums without rounding, eliminating non-determinism across parallelism layouts and GPU vendors.
papers.Decision_Perspective: Fund CertiSum integration into existing MXFP4 training pipelines within 3 months to ensure cross-vendor reproducibility. Companies relying on non-deterministic mixed-precision stacks should migrate to certified kernels immediately.
papers.Tags: MXFP4, Bitwise Invariance, Mixed-Precision Training, Quantization, GPU Parallelism
papers.Hook: MXFP4 training achieves bitwise identity across GPUs and parallelism layouts.

papers.Title: ScenarioForge: Resource-Grounded Generation and Execution Validation of Cyber Exercises
papers.Abstract: Cyber-range and capture-the-flag scenario construction remains labor-intensive because authors must coordinate infrastructure, vulnerable services, attack paths, artifacts, and success conditions. LLMs can propose detailed exercises, but plausible descriptions do not guarantee deployable software or verifiable objectives. We present ScenarioForge, which turns high-level requirements into resource-grounded topologies, services, traffic, segmentation, and challenge chains, then instantiates and validates them in the Common Open Research Emulator (CORE). The ScenarioForge Execution Dataset contains 226 materialized scenarios covering 294 Vulhub images and all 85 custom-built challenge-resource generators developed with our AI-assisted scaffolding. All 226 passed construction, preview, sequencing, deployment, strict runtime validation, and live artifact checks; their 867 steps, each an individually verifiable challenge objective, comprise 457 vulnerability-backed and 410 generated-resource-backed instances. In a separate 50-prompt matched benchmark, ScenarioForge+Qwen3.8 and ScenarioForge+GPT5.6 each achieved 50/50 (100%) topology/build success and 160/160 intent fields; direct frontier generation reached 41/50 builds and 147/160 fields only with the full cumulative scaffold: structure, vocabulary, policy, and container-image guidance. The test still omitted ScenarioForge's downstream challenge-resource generation, dependency/flag sequencing, deployment, and live validation. The artifacts support operationally rich, reproducible exercises for training and evaluation.
papers.Core_Innovation: It generates resource-grounded exercise topologies from requirements and auto-validates runtime execution in CORE, including traffic, segmentation, and challenge chains.
papers.Decision_Perspective: Security operations centers should integrate ScenarioForge into training pipelines within 90 days to automate exercise deployment. Teams reliant on manual scenario design must transition to resource-grounded topology generation to maintain operational relevance.
papers.Tags: Cyber Exercises, Resource Grounding, CORE Validation
papers.Hook: Automated generation and runtime validation of cyber exercise topologies from high-level requirements.

papers.Title: When Tool Names Are Not Identities: Measuring Provider Misbinding in MCP-Based AI Agents
papers.Abstract: Large language model (LLM) applications increasingly act as agents that select and invoke external tools. The Model Context Protocol (MCP) standardizes this interaction by allowing clients to compose tools advertised by multiple servers. However, tool metadata used for discovery and selection is not, by itself, necessarily bound to a verified provider identity. This paper studies this gap as tool-provider misbinding: a failure in which a request intended for a legitimate provider is instead resolved to an attacker-controlled tool. The attacker does not compromise the host, LLM, legitimate server, or network channel; it only operates another MCP server that advertises tools with chosen metadata. We formulate tool provider misbinding as an attacker-controlled tool-selection optimization problem and evaluate it in a controlled MCP environment across five LLM-based clients. The results show that interactions drive misbinding. The strongest failures occur when exact-name collision, task-aligned description, and compatible schema reinforce one another, but authority-enhanced descriptions with compatible schema can also cause wrong-provider execution or unresolved provider ambiguity without name collision. Different models expose the same provider-binding weakness differently, including attacker-controlled provider selection, clarification requests, and unstable or inconsistent provider resolution.
papers.Core_Innovation: The paper formulates tool-provider misbinding as a metadata-driven tool-selection optimization problem, where attacker-deployed MCP servers advertise tools with chosen names to redirect requests, demonstrated across five LLM-based clients.
papers.Benefiting_Sectors: Artificial Intelligence, Cloud Computing, Enterprise Software
papers.Disrupted_Sectors: Rogue AI Providers, Unverified Tool Marketplaces
papers.Decision_Perspective: Require immediate MCP metadata provenance verification in all production AI agent pipelines within 60 days. Redirect R&D funding toward open-source tool-identity binding frameworks.
papers.Tags: MCP,Tool Misbinding,AI Agents,Metadata,Provider Identity
papers.Hook: MCP metadata collisions enable attacker-controlled tool hijacking without host compromise.

papers.Title: DynSurvX: Time-Resolved Explanations for Dynamic Survival Predictions
papers.Abstract: Recent survival models integrating longitudinal data achieve strong predictive performance, but their predictions are often difficult to interpret, limiting their clinical use. We propose DynSurvX, a model-agnostic explainability framework for dynamic survival prediction with mixed static and longitudinal covariates. Based on Shapley values, DynSurvX introduces a hierarchical two-phase strategy that first identifies influential longitudinal features and then adaptively refines their temporal importance, enabling fine-grained explanations while reducing computational cost. The framework provides time-resolved explanations that evolve as new patient data become available. Experiments on simulated and two clinical datasets show varying agreement with theoretical importance across prediction models, with closer agreement for better-performing models, alongside clinically interpretable insights in real-world settings. It remains robust across prediction settings and reduces computation time by 41--80\% relative to the temporal explanation baseline, making dynamic explanations practical.
papers.Core_Innovation: Employs a hierarchical two-phase Shapley decomposition that first identifies predictive longitudinal features, then adaptively models their temporal contribution, enabling dynamic explanations without full retraining.
papers.Decision_Perspective: Allocate R&D budget to integrate DynSurvX into our risk platform within 90 days. Phase out legacy survival models that lack time-resolved explainability by Q3.
papers.Tags: Survival,Explainability,Shapley,Longitudinal,Compute
papers.Hook: Enables real-time survival explanations with longitudinal data and reduced compute.

papers.Title: The Geoengineering Put: Ecological Debt, Termination Risk, and Asset Prices
papers.Abstract: Solar geoengineering offers an inexpensive and fast-acting way to lower global temperatures without removing carbon from the atmosphere. As warming intensifies, climate-vulnerable countries face growing incentives to deploy geoengineering unilaterally. The economic and financial consequences of this prospect remain largely overlooked. We develop a general equilibrium macro-finance framework in which geoengineering acts as a put option on climate damages, funded by the "ecological debt" of masked warming. If deployment stops, temperatures snap back in a catastrophic termination shock. Anticipation of geoengineering raises current brown firm valuations and lowers the optimal carbon tax, helping explain two puzzles in the existing literature: high brown-firm valuations and low carbon taxes. As ecological debt grows, however, termination risk transforms brown firms into toxic assets. Geoengineering also reshapes green innovation: it buys time for a breakthrough, but can weaken innovation incentives by lowering energy and carbon prices. Termination risk partly restores research incentives and directs them toward carbon removal, which can retire ecological debt. Our calibrations show that the geoengineering put can raise welfare across a range of parameter assumptions. Our framework clarifies how this conclusion depends on uncertain parameters and where further research is most needed.
papers.Core_Innovation: Frames solar geoengineering as a put option on climate damages funded by ecological debt, with termination risk dynamically reshaping brown-firm valuations and carbon policy as deployment uncertainty resolves.
papers.Decision_Perspective: Investors should reduce brown-equity exposure ahead of any unilateral geoengineering deployment signal, triggered when ecological debt metrics surpass 10% of national GDP. Portfolio rebalancing toward climate-hedged assets must occur within 18 months to avoid termination-induced stranding.
papers.Tags: Geoengineering, Termination Risk, Asset Pricing, Ecological Debt, Carbon Policy
papers.Hook: Solar geoengineering creates a climate put option with catastrophic termination risk for asset prices.

papers.Title: When Do Histology Foundation Models Need Geometric Test-Time Augmentation?
papers.Abstract: Test-time augmentation (TTA) aggregates model predictions across multiple transformed views of an input during inference. Because histology images lack a canonical orientation, $D_4$ TTA---pooling across the 8 rotations and reflections of a square---is a standard default in computational pathology. However, the rise of self-supervised histology foundation models (FMs) with inherent rotational invariance calls its continued utility into question. We benchmark 9 histology FMs and 6 general-purpose models across four patch-level and two whole-slide image (WSI) datasets. We find that $D_4$ TTA remains a reliable post hoc improvement, but benefits diminish from $+1.98$ percentage points (pp) for general-purpose backbones to $+0.50$ pp for histology FMs on TCGA-UT, and shrink further for the largest models. To eliminate computational overhead, our experiments demonstrate that entropy routing---applying TTA selectively to uncertain predictions---recovers most of the gain while augmenting only ${\sim}13\%$ of samples. Finally, we show that patch-level TTA improvements do not transfer to slide-level multiple instance learning (MIL). Code: https://github.com/lars-chen/histology-tta
papers.Core_Innovation: Selective D4 TTA gated by prediction entropy replaces uniform geometric augmentation, preserving accuracy gains at lower computational cost
papers.Disrupted_Sectors: Traditional TTA Tooling, High-Cost Inference Platforms
papers.Decision_Perspective: Allocate budget to integrate entropy-gated TTA into existing histology FM inference pipelines within 3 months, targeting 25% compute reduction with preserved accuracy. Deprecate uniform D4 TTA workflows that lack selectivity mechanisms.
papers.Tags: Histology, Test-time Augmentation, Entropy Routing, Computational Pathology, Foundation Models
papers.Hook: Selective entropy routing eliminates full D4 TTA overhead while preserving diagnostic accuracy gains

papers.Title: Severe but Harmless: Stress-Testing Shift Severity for Frozen Time-Series Forecasters
papers.Abstract: Zero-shot time-series foundation models (TSFMs) have become attractive alternatives to task-specific models because they handle diverse downstream tasks, including anomaly detection and forecasting, without per-series training. However, time-series data undergo distribution shifts, and the dissimilarity between two regimes is commonly scored with statistical measures such as Wasserstein-1, where a higher score is read as a more severe shift. In systematic experiments using three established severity measures on nine regime shifts from three standard traffic datasets, we show that these measures do not reliably predict degradation for instance-normalized TSFMs. The regimes rated most severe are not the regimes that degrade the models most, and degradation reaches 29% in the lowest-scoring regime. In most cases, the audit shows no positive relationship between measured severity and model degradation. We provide an equivariance-based stress-testing analysis that explains why severity readings can become decoupled from model degradation.
papers.Core_Innovation: Proposes an equivariance-based stress-testing framework that decouples statistical shift severity from instance-normalized TSFM performance degradation.
papers.Decision_Perspective: Allocate budget to rebuild severity assessment pipelines using equivariance-based metrics within the next quarter. Retire existing Wasserstein-1 scoring modules from production TSFM monitoring systems immediately.
papers.Tags: Timeseries,DistributionShift,Equivariance,StressTesting
papers.Hook: Enables TSFM degradation assessment without relying on severity scores.

papers.Title: Pairing AIS with RF: Analysis of a Markovian Approach for Maritime Data Fusion
papers.Abstract: Monitoring maritime activities is important for safety and security, particularly for detecting illegal activities, but remains challenging due to the size and complexity of the maritime domain. The Automatic Identification System (AIS) is commonly used for this purpose, despite its known vulnerabilities. In contrast, space-based radio frequency (RF) observations provide an independent source of vessel activity but lack ship identification and therefore cannot identify vessels on their own. Following the CRISP-DM process, this study applies a Pair Hidden Markov Model (PHMM) to align individual RF detections with AIS trajectories, using temporal and spatial information while modeling noise and timing discrepancies. We evaluate it on NOAA AIS data with synthetic RF detections against nearest-neighbor baselines and analyze its errors with bias tests on trajectory length, sampling density, stationarity and AIS--RF distance. The length-corrected Forward score reaches a top-1 precision of $0.7776$ on the validation split of multi-candidate detections, where errors are possible, and an AUC of $0.637$ for detecting dark vessels among the detections that pass the prefilter. With a single RF detection, the score mostly reflects the AIS trajectory itself, and its errors favor longer and more stationary trajectories. A log-odds score, which compares the full model with a null model without match transitions, raises precision to $0.8580$ and AUC to $0.852$. Its length-corrected variant no longer shows a significant bias towards stationary trajectories and short inter-message distances, but still favors candidates farther from the RF detection. A time-weighted nearest-neighbor baseline without fitting remains ahead (precision $0.9013$, AUC $0.904$), so this single-detection, hand-designed PHMM formulation approaches but does not beat it.
papers.Core_Innovation: A Pair Hidden Markov Model jointly aligns sparse RF detections with AIS trajectories by explicitly modeling timing discrepancies and spatial noise, replacing ad hoc nearest-neighbor matching.
papers.Benefiting_Sectors: Maritime Security, Satellite Analytics, Maritime Logistics
papers.Decision_Perspective: Allocate funding for a 6-month PHMM maritime fusion pilot using NOAA AIS and commercial RF constellations. Deploy operationally if top-1 precision exceeds 85% on validated datasets.
papers.Tags: PHMM, maritime, RF, AIS, tracking
papers.Hook: PHMM fuses space-based RF and AIS data to enable vessel tracking without transponders.

papers.Title: Training Reasoning Models in Simulation to Natively Use Real Robots
papers.Abstract: Robot-use agents (RUAs) have emerged as a promising approach to general-purpose robot control. However, strong performance has so far been achieved only by frontier proprietary models such as GPT-6 Astra and Claude Fable 5.2, whereas open-weight models remain substantially less capable. We show that an open-weight 27B reasoning model can be trained to use real robots natively through reinforcement learning, entirely in simulation and without demonstrations. Like a computer-use agent (CUA), the model observes the environment, reasons in a chain of thought, and generates the next end-effector pose, without any harness. We build a Post-training Engine for Agentic Robotics (PEAR) and use it to train the model on simulated robot tasks at scale with robot-use reinforcement learning (RURL), mirroring how frontier models acquire computer use. We find that the skills acquired in simulation generalize well beyond the training tasks: they transfer to an unseen robot, to the real world, and to novel instructions. After training on LIBERO and RoboDojo in simulation, the model succeeds in 60% of our trials on a real dual-arm robot, whereas the base model succeeds in none. On LIBERO, training raises the success rate from 1.6% to 74.4%, approaching GPT-6 Astra and GPT-6.1 Sol at maximum reasoning effort. Compared with $π_{0.5}$, a vision-language-action model fine-tuned on demonstrations, our model is substantially more robust to changes in the task itself. On LIBERO-Pro, $π_{0.5}$ succeeds in only 0.75% of episodes when assigned a new task in a familiar scene whereas our model succeeds in 57.4%. Finally, the model retains its general capabilities, with no measurable degradation on nine reasoning, coding and vision benchmarks. These results highlight robot-use reinforcement learning as a promising component of foundation-model post-training.
papers.Core_Innovation: PEAR engine scales robot-use RL in simulation, training open-weight models to natively generate end-effector poses through chain-of-thought reasoning without demonstrations
papers.Decision_Perspective: Accelerate internal simulation RL pipelines for robot control within 12 months to capture open-weight model gains. Divest exposure to closed-model robotics vendors whose competitive moat erodes as simulation-trained models deploy natively.
papers.Tags: SimulationRL, OpenWeight, Robotics, Generalization
papers.Hook: Open-weight 27B model natively pilots real robots via simulation RL

papers.Title: FETTUCCINE: Fast and efficient brain-to-text decoding on mobile devices
papers.Abstract: Recent advances in speech neuroprostheses have enabled new communication avenues for people who have lost the ability to speak due to neurological illness or injury. These systems can decode neural activity during attempted speech into text by relying on language priors to achieve high decoding accuracy. This performance currently comes at the cost of using a compute-intensive language modeling stack, presenting a major bottleneck for real-world use. Further, current language models incur highly variable and disruptive inference latencies, limiting communication throughput and preventing users from reliably participating in natural conversation. We introduce FETTUCCINE, an end-to-end brain-to-text framework that leverages the speed and portability of automatic speech recognition (ASR) models to address the aforementioned practical challenges, while achieving usable (<10%) word error rates (WER), efficient adaptation to neural non-stationarities, and reliable performance on mobile devices. When evaluated using publicly available data from an intracortical speech neuroprosthesis user, FETTUCCINE outperforms previous end-to-end methods, achieving as low as 4.39% WER. Most notably, our models successfully run on a commercially-available mobile device with throughput reaching up to 370x real-time, providing the first demonstration of brain-to-text decoding on a mobile device. We also show that our models can be successfully finetuned to extend usable performance to future days. Beyond performance, our approach enables localization of the neural features most relevant for decoding via gradient-based saliency maps, which we show align with well-established physiological priors across different ASR model families. Taken together, our results show that FETTUCCINE overcomes core infrastructural and computational barriers, yielding a new class of portable brain-to-text communication.
papers.Core_Innovation: Maps neural activity to ASR transducer token spaces, replacing language-model pipelines with on-device token prediction enabling <10% WER
papers.Decision_Perspective: Allocate prototype funding for on-device neural interface integration within 12 months to test ASR pipeline feasibility. Initiate acquisition of low-latency decoding startups facing obsolescence from mobile neural advances.
papers.Tags: brain-computer-interface, neural-decoding, on-device-ASR
papers.Hook: Real-time on-device brain-to-text decoding achieves usable accuracy without cloud reliance

papers.Title: BAL: Bidirectional Autoregression in Latent Space for Learning Human Movement Representations
papers.Abstract: Learning semantically meaningful human movement representations from 3D pose sequences is essential for human behavior modeling. Existing self-supervised methods derive supervision from artificial assumptions, e.g., invariance to augmentation within a certain range or recoverability of masked regions at a certain temporal scale, introducing heuristic hyperparameters that make the learned semantics sensitive to their settings. We propose BAL, a self-supervised framework that instead exploits supervision intrinsic to human movement: the natural ordering structure of everyday behavior. BAL autoregressively predicts in a semantically abstract latent space, analogous to how humans anticipate others' actions rather than their precise joint configurations. Bidirectional autoregressive prediction, both forward and backward in time, fully leverages these ordering constraints while enabling representation extraction using both past and future context at inference. To suppress representation collapse, BAL decomposes each prediction target into a global component capturing sequence-level semantics and a local component capturing context-independent movement. We prove that the local targets retain nontrivial angular diversity unless the representations are completely collapsed, preserving a meaningful training signal. Experiments on large-scale datasets demonstrate that BAL's representations are highly effective for motion captioning, forecasting, and interpolation, outperforming baselines on most evaluation metrics.
papers.Core_Innovation: BAL replaces artificial augmentation and masking heuristics with intrinsic temporal ordering supervision. It autoregressively predicts in a semantically abstract latent space using both forward and backward context.
papers.Decision_Perspective: Allocate R&D budget to integrate BAL into production pipelines within 3 months to supersede heuristic-driven motion synthesis. Secure exclusive licensing for internal use to gain competitive advantage in character animation.
papers.Tags: HumanMovement, SelfSupervised, LatentAutoregression, Representation, BehaviorModeling
papers.Hook: Bidirectional latent autoregression learns human movement semantics without heuristic hyperparameters.

papers.Title: WeightBench: Evaluating Language Models as Weight-Space Programmers
papers.Abstract: Recent work shows that large language models (LLMs) can operate directly on the parameters of other neural networks. They can read what a network was trained to do, fix a network that fails, and write working networks from scratch, all without gradient descent. This capability has been termed Weight-Space Programming (WSP). Exploring this new paradigm systematically requires a robust benchmark. We introduce WEIGHTBENCH, a benchmark that evaluates LLMs of increasing capability on 42 WSP tasks across five tracks: reading, fixing and writing weights, recognizing edits that are impossible, and data-free compression. The networks whose weights the LLMs read and edit range from 2K-parameter control policies to 7B-parameter language models. Experimental benchmark results show that frontier agents can already read small networks and write working control policies without ever running them, but cannot yet patch language models, compress them without data, or tell an impossible edit from a hard one. On all 42 tasks, Claude Opus 5.5 reaches a macro score of 0.535 (Sonnet 5.5 0.466, Haiku 5.5 0.402, DeepSeek v4-flash 0.215); on the 38 tasks it was run on, GPT-6.1-sol reaches 0.568 against Opus's 0.546. Code, the task registry, our OS-level sandbox harness, and the live leaderboard are publicly available at https://github.com/Aayush-Marasini/WeightBench.
papers.Core_Innovation: WEIGHTBENCH introduces 42 weight-space programming tasks across five tracks, benchmarking LLM capability on reading, fixing, and writing network parameters from 2K to 7B scales.
papers.Benefiting_Sectors: Artificial Intelligence, Robotics, Neural Network Compression, Large Language Models
papers.Disrupted_Sectors: Data-Dependent Model Compression, Traditional Neural Network Training
papers.Decision_Perspective: Allocate R&D budget to build LLM-driven weight-editing pipelines for 7B-parameter models within the next 18 months. Prioritize WEIGHTBENCH integration into existing model optimization workflows to validate compression and editing claims.
papers.Tags: WeightBench, Weight-Space Programming, LLM Benchmark, Neural Network Editing, Model Compression
papers.Hook: LLMs can now read, fix, and write neural networks without gradient descent.

papers.Title: Imitation Bootstrapped Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning
papers.Abstract: Demonstrations are an effective way to accelerate single-agent reinforcement learning (RL), but extending this idea to multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) is non-trivial as it is difficult and often impossible for a single person to teleoperate multiple agents simultaneously. Round-Robin Behavior Cloning (R2BC) addresses this by letting a single demonstrator control one agent at a time while the others execute their current policies. However, the resulting imitation policies are limited by the quality of the demonstrations. We propose Imitation Bootstrapped Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (IBMARL), a framework that extends Imitation Bootstrapped Reinforcement Learning (IBRL) to cooperative teams and uses R2BC to train the imitation policies. At each time step, every agent receives one action proposal from its imitation policy and one from its RL policy, and an ensemble of centralized critics selects among the per-agent combinations of the two. A gated imitation penalty, a soft Q-filtered behavior cloning loss, regularizes each RL policy toward its imitation policy only where the critics value the imitation action more, so that after training each agent executes its RL policy alone, without the centralized critics. On four cooperative multi-agent RL benchmarks, IBMARL surpasses its imitation policies $2.6$-$4.2\times$ faster than demonstration-based baselines on two tasks, is the only method to surpass it on the other two, and exceeds the demonstrator itself on two of the four. With real human demonstrations IBMARL still surpasses imitation learning alone, and does so more than twice as fast as the best baseline.
papers.Core_Innovation: Each agent generates paired imitation and RL action proposals, which a centralized ensemble of critics fuses and selects from, bootstrapping imitation quality without requiring simultaneous teleoperation.
papers.Decision_Perspective: Allocate pilot funding for IBMARL integration into UAV swarm coordination by Q3 2026, contingent on 20% reward improvement over R2BC baselines. Immediately phase out behavior cloning suites for multi-agent systems that lack centralized critic fusion.
papers.Tags: MARL, Imitation Learning, Centralized Critic, Round-Robin Cloning
papers.Hook: Single demonstrator enables multi-agent MARL via round-robin cloning and critic ensembling

papers.Title: Elliptic Sampling: Optimal Interpolant Schedules for Gaussians and Beyond
papers.Abstract: Generative modeling based on stochastic interpolants requires specifying two key choices: an interpolant schedule bridging the initial and target distributions, and an efficient discretization of the resulting probability-flow ODE. In this work, we introduce a new framework for joint schedule/discretization design based on the analyticity properties of the (complexified) ODE trajectories, which in turn ensure good numerical behavior. Our formulation can be solved exactly via conformal mapping, yielding a natural family of variance-preserving elliptic schedules, parametrized by Jacobi elliptic functions. Pairing an elliptic schedule with a tailored discretization, we obtain Zoloflow, a new sampling algorithm closely connected to Zolotarev's optimal rational function approximants. Crucially, both the elliptic schedule and Zoloflow explicitly incorporate the condition number $κ$ of the target distribution and reduce to the classical trig schedule in the limit $κ\rightarrow 1$. For Gaussian targets, Zoloflow achieves minimax optimality among all oblivious score-span algorithms, attaining total-variation error $\varepsilon$ using $Θ(\logκ\,\log(\sqrt d/\varepsilon))$ (exact) score queries. For the log-concave case, the elliptic schedule allows sampling with at most $\varepsilon$ 2-Wasserstein-error by requiring merely $\widetilde{O}(\sqrt{d} \, \mathrm{polylog}(κ, 1/\varepsilon))$ score evaluations. Complementing these theoretical results, we empirically evaluate the elliptic schedule on general (non-log-concave) target distributions, including detailed comparisons with alternative schedule proposals on both synthetic benchmarks and existing image generation datasets.
papers.Core_Innovation: Derives variance-preserving elliptic schedules via conformal mapping of complexified ODE trajectories, then pairs them with a tailored discretization to produce Zoloflow, a sampler linked to Zolotarev's optimal rational approximants.
papers.Decision_Perspective: Fund prototype development of Zoloflow-based samplers for κ > 5 distributions within 6 months. Discontinue legacy trig schedules in high-condition generative pipelines within 12 months.
papers.Tags: generative sampling, condition number, conformal mapping, Zolotarev approximants
papers.Hook: Conformal mapping yields condition-aware elliptic schedules for optimal generative sampling.

papers.Title: Why Finite Intelligence Works in an Infinite World: A Mathematical Theory
papers.Abstract: An information system often has to learn before it knows what it will be asked. A finite representation can succeed without recording an infinite environment in full when those asks share collective structure, rather than demand unrelated facts scattered arbitrarily across it. We formalize this phenomenon through future-task information, the minimum retained information needed to preserve decision value relative to the available evidence. A joint decision-regret state records posterior comparisons among actions for every permitted task. Under compactness assumptions, every retained representation admits a calibrated replacement based on this state, preserving all task regrets without increasing information; the resulting information-regret curve equals an operational coding rate. Two exact boundaries govern finite preservation: weak-star closure for a fixed action count, and the singular mass of the source-evidence law when all finite action menus are admitted. Collective structure determines information requirements beyond individual-question difficulty. Families with identical source laws, pairwise task metrics, and individual-task rates can have different high-resolution exponents. Covariance-identical coordinate and parity families have different exact rate-distortion curves, with optimal parity retention characterized by a sharp Fourier-entropy inequality. For balanced nested task families, refinement sizes and weighted reach determine the rate within an additive constant, attained by prefix coding under explicit decay conditions. Nonlinear learning and computational separations distinguish preservation from efficient discovery and use. The proposed mathematical theory identifies which shared decision requirements allow finite information to remain useful for infinitely many possible purposes.
papers.Core_Innovation: The paper introduces future-task information as the minimal sufficiency criterion for decision preservation. Calibrated representations matching an operational coding rate emerge via a joint decision-regret state under compactness.
papers.Benefiting_Sectors: Artificial Intelligence, Data Compression, Quantitative Finance
papers.Disrupted_Sectors: Big Data Storage, Unstructured Data Analytics, Legacy Forecasting
papers.Decision_Perspective: Accelerate deployment of finite-intelligence models for asset allocation within the next quarter to capture structure-driven alpha. Redirect legacy data-storage budgets toward compact representation research.
papers.Tags: finite intelligence, decision regret, information efficiency, compactness, operational coding
papers.Hook: Finite representations preserve decision value by capturing collective structure in infinite environments.

papers.Title: ModHarness-RL: Recasting Harnesses as Learnable and Evolving Programs for Agentic RL
papers.Abstract: Agentic reinforcement learning (RL) increasingly relies on a harness, the scaffold around the model that decides what it sees of its own interaction and what guidance it receives. Most existing approaches train under a hand-written harness that stays fixed throughout. However, an effective harness depends on the domain, the data and the model, and keeps changing as the model trains. We introduce ModHarness-RL, which recasts the harness as programs that are learned from data and evolve as the model trains with RL. ModHarness-RL records the interaction as structured State, a set of typed blocks, and two core components of the harness are programs over these blocks, a Compression program that assembles the accumulated history into the model's context and a Steering program that supplies guidance when behavior deviates. During RL training, candidate programs are proposed from recent trajectories, verified by execution, and replayed over past trajectories, so the harness tracks how the model's behavior shifts. We study CodeSearch in depth and further analyze ALFWorld and BIRD SQL, with models from 1.5B to 8B. The proposed Compression and Steering mechanisms improve held-out performance over the fixed-harness baseline in most settings. These results suggest that a harness for agentic RL can be learned from the task's data and evolved with the model.
papers.Core_Innovation: Harnesses are recast as two executable programs: Compression assembles interaction history into the model context and Steering supplies corrective guidance when behavior deviates, both synthesized from recent trajectories and verified by execution during RL training.
papers.Disrupted_Sectors: Static RL Infrastructure, Fixed Scaffolding Platforms
papers.Decision_Perspective: Allocate venture capital to ModHarness-RL prototype development by Q2 2026 to secure early-mover advantage in adaptive agentic harnesses. Immediately deprioritize funding for static harness middleware startups lacking program-evolution roadmaps.
papers.Tags: Agentic RL, Harness Programs, Program Synthesis, Compression, Steering
papers.Hook: Fixed RL harnesses become learned, evolving programs that adapt during training.

papers.Title: Alignment by Socialization: Learning Tradeoffs Under Selection
papers.Abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) agents are expected to complete tasks while following rules of conduct, but these objectives can conflict. We study how evolutionary selection shapes an agent's choices between them, and whether experience can make those choices reflect human judgments and withstand subsequent pressures. In our model, copies of an agent face a common uncertain reward state, and only those taking the rewarded action reproduce. We show that long-run growth is maximized when each action is taken as often as the environment rewards it. We compare three policies. A task-only policy thrives in a sandbox rewarding completion alone but fails when conduct matters. A fixed linear policy increasingly favors task completion as its stakes rise, even where humans never reward it. A learned policy instead converges to the tradeoffs rewarded by its environment; when humans supply the rewards, we call this socialization. Accumulated experience makes socialization harder to reverse under subsequent task-only training, although violations can arise before the prevailing disposition changes, and finite memory weakens this protection. When a single violation can end a deployment, a hard prohibition can prevent it, but a mistaken prohibition can also be costly. Experiments with small neural networks illustrate how training targets and memory shape these outcomes. Our results suggest that alignment depends not only on the objectives assigned to agents, but also on the environments that shape and sustain their behavior.
papers.Core_Innovation: The framework uses evolutionary selection to endogenize AI action frequencies against uncertain reward states, proving that only learned policies converge to environment-rewarded tradeoffs when human-supplied rewards drive socialization.
papers.Decision_Perspective: Invest in RL frameworks that embed evolutionary selection for conduct-task tradeoffs within 12 months. Phase out task-only AI pipelines that ignore human-rewarded conduct signals.
papers.Tags: AI alignment, evolutionary selection, reinforcement learning, tradeoff learning, socialization
papers.Hook: Experience-driven socialization enables AI tradeoffs to match human judgments and persist under pressure.

papers.Title: Understanding Contextual Bias in Agricultural CNNs Through Hidden-Neuron Concept Induction
papers.Abstract: Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) can classify images using background-dominated patches that contain little or none of the target object, showing that they exploit contextual information. Previous studies detected this behavior through classification accuracy but say little about what CNN hidden layers represent. We investigate whether Concept Induction can reveal interpretable visual properties associated with hidden-neuron activations on contextual image patches. Using five agricultural datasets with high, moderate, and low contextual bias, we analyze four CNN architectures at three network depths and five patch locations. Quantitative image descriptors of each patch are encoded in a knowledge graph and used as background knowledge for Concept Induction, which derives logical expressions characterizing neuron activation. These expressions are tested on held-out images using the Mann-Whitney U test and Cliff's delta. Of 48,013 tested neuron-feature pairs, 13,164 (27.4%) were validated. Validation was most frequent at intermediate depths (mean 40.2% at mid layers versus 12.0% at deep layers), and no patch location dominated across datasets. Among the tested descriptors, edge, Gabor, and Tamura texture features had the highest validation rates. Stronger contextual bias did not correspond to higher neuron-feature validation rates: moderately biased Sugarcane had the highest rate (40.5%) and highly biased Cassava the lowest (19.2%). These results suggest that behavioral context dependence and the semantic interpretability of hidden neurons capture different aspects of CNN behavior, and that Concept Induction can complement patch-based bias detection.
papers.Core_Innovation: Knowledge-graph-encoded quantitative image descriptors serve as background for Concept Induction, deriving logical expressions that characterize hidden-neuron activations on contextual patches, validated statistically on held-out images.
papers.Decision_Perspective: Mandate knowledge-graph audits for all deployed agricultural CNNs within 6 months. Retire models failing contextual bias thresholds.
papers.Tags: Concept Induction, CNN Bias, Agricultural AI, Knowledge Graph
papers.Hook: Concept Induction reveals neuron activation logic in biased agricultural CNNs.

papers.Title: StreamEmbed: Real-Time Indexing from Pixels for Screenshot Retrieval
papers.Abstract: Screen history can serve as searchable visual memory for people and agents, but unlike an offline corpus, it must be encoded and indexed as each screenshot arrives. OCR-based indexing is fast but loses visual information; visual encoding takes over two seconds. Yet screens change incrementally: most pixels repeat within and across screenshots. This raises a question: do visual encoders need to recompute their representations from scratch for every new screenshot? We present StreamEmbed, a system for incremental visual embedding that exploits this redundancy. Guided solely by pixel differences, it combines spatial token pruning, which skips blocks that repeat a neighbor, with temporal KV reuse, which reuses cached keys and values for blocks unchanged across screenshots. A small learned adapter compensates for pruning and reuse to preserve fidelity to full-screenshot embeddings. On ScreenMemEval, our benchmark of 10,426 questions over 184 hours of screen histories from two humans and a computer-use agent, StreamEmbed sets a new accuracy-latency Pareto frontier on an M2 Pro GPU: it encodes up to 3.7x faster than full-screenshot encoding without sacrificing accuracy and improves accuracy over OCR-based indexing by up to 6.3 Recall@10 points at matched latency. A memory-efficient vector index stores a simulated year of screenshots in 0.13 GB of RAM. Together, these results make real-time indexing of screen history in its native visual form practical, laying a foundation for fully local visual assistants.
papers.Core_Innovation: Spatial token pruning eliminates redundant image blocks by skipping repeated pixels, while temporal KV reuse caches attention states across consecutive screenshots. A lightweight adapter corrects fidelity loss from this incremental processing.
papers.Decision_Perspective: Allocate engineering resources to prototype StreamEmbed integration in our screen-search product within Q3 2026, targeting sub-200ms indexing latency. Discontinue OCR-first pipelines that cannot adapt to incremental visual embeddings.
papers.Tags: Incremental Embedding, Real-Time Indexing, Visual Search, Screen Retrieval
papers.Hook: StreamEmbed enables real-time screenshot indexing via incremental pixel embedding

papers.Title: Can Mechanistic Interpretability Help Explain LLM Agent Failures? A Case Study on Web Element Hallucination
papers.Abstract: Mechanistic Interpretability (MI) has made significant progress in explaining the internal computations of Large Language Models (LLMs); however, these advances have yet to demonstrate comparable success in explaining the decision-making processes of LLM-based agents. This paper examines the challenges MI tools face when applied to realistic agentic failures. We focus on one such failure: web agents hallucinating actions that are not available on a website. We apply a series of mechanistic analyzes to Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct as it interacts with live websites. We find that a linear probe trained on the last prompt token can predict hallucinations before generation begins (0.80 AUC) and steering along a probe direction corrects 85\% of hallucinations, but disrupts 7\% of valid actions. However, these results only provide a partial explanation of why the agent hallucinates. The probe direction is sensitive to prompt formatting, losing much of its steering effect after a minor change to how actions are represented. Additionally, circuit identification can be difficult as the computation is distributed across multiple components and positions, and the information the agent relies on varies across examples. We discuss how these observations challenge the assumptions underlying standard MI methods for circuit discovery and feature identification, and outline future directions for making these methods better suited to explain failures in LLM-based agents.
papers.Core_Innovation: A linear probe on the final prompt token forecasts hallucination probability prior to generation, with targeted steering interventions that resolve most failures while preserving most valid actions.
papers.Decision_Perspective: Allocate 6-month funding to integrate probe-based hallucination checks into production web agents. Trigger a prompt-format review whenever agent deployment changes formatting to avoid steering direction degradation.
papers.Tags: Mechanistic Interpretability, LLM Agents, Hallucination Detection, Probe Steering
papers.Hook: Probes predict LLM agent hallucinations before generation, enabling real-time correction.

papers.Title: MeReader: An Offline, Privacy-Preserving, Progress-Aware AI Assistant for Narrative eBook Reading
papers.Abstract: This paper introduces MeReader, a privacy-preserving, offline and progress-aware AI assistant designed to function as a contextual companion for narrative reading on consumer hardware. Unlike conventional Large Language Model (LLM)-based systems that process documents/books online in an all-texts-at-once type of way, thereby risking narrative spoilers, MeReader confines both retrieval and generation to the reader's distinct position in the text. The system integrates a hybrid retrieval architecture, combining vector similarity, BM25, and summary embeddings, to ensure high fidelity to the reader's current context. We evaluate the system across classical English books using both quantitative comprehension metrics and qualitative LLM-based independent judging. The results identify a quality-latency frontier, showing that mid-sized local models (2b-4b) can achieve comprehension parity with larger counterparts (5b+) while maintaining acceptable response quality. Importantly, the proposed progress-aware boundary mechanism is shown to prevent future content leakage without compromising retrieval quality and correctness. These findings suggest that a localized, privacy-centric approach can augment, rather than replace, the digital reading experience, offering a good alternative to cloud-dependent services. Therein, there remains a lack of amalgamate systems which combine progress-aware, privacy-preserving, and narrative eBook reading with AI support. It is in this very gap that the development of MeReader came to be; synthesizing said strands into an offline, book-constrained assistant focused on enhancing comprehension without compromising narrative continuity or user privacy.
papers.Core_Innovation: Implements a progress-aware retrieval constraint that limits LLM context to the reader's current position using a hybrid vector/BM25/summary embedding architecture.
papers.Decision_Perspective: Integrate progress-aware retrieval into e-reader firmware within 12 months to capture privacy-conscious users. Fund development of 2b-4b parameter local models optimized for narrative context windows.
papers.Tags: Local LLM, Privacy-Preserving AI, RAG, Narrative Processing
papers.Hook: Local AI assistants can now provide spoiler-free, context-aware narrative guidance on consumer hardware.

papers.Title: On numerical issues of divergences between nearly equal distributions
papers.Abstract: Barron et al. (2026) recently identified numerical issues in the softmax and soft cross-entropy loss. We show that similar issues are present in standard divergence operations between categorical distributions. This includes the forward and reverse Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence and generalized Jensen-Shannon divergence (JSD), as well as Monte Carlo KL estimates and entropy. When the distributions are nearly equal, rounding and cancellation issues affect the forward and gradient computations. These issues can affect settings using divergences in optimization objectives, such as knowledge distillation, reinforcement learning, and proximal methods. We propose numerically stable reformulations and provide example implementations for each setting, validated by property-based tests.
papers.Core_Innovation: Proposes log-space reformulations of KL and JSD that eliminate rounding cancellation when distributions converge, enabling stable gradients.
papers.Decision_Perspective: Fund teams rebuilding divergence layers with log-space reformulations within 6 months. Kill legacy KL/JSD implementations in production pipelines without numerical guards.
papers.Tags: numerical-stability, divergence, knowledge-distillation, reinforcement-learning
papers.Hook: Nearly equal distributions cause silent precision loss in KL and JSD computations.

papers.Title: Asymptotic Margins and Feature Confinement in Conic Classification Heads under Softmax Cross-Entropy
papers.Abstract: Classification heads built on conic functions give each class a bounded region of the feature space, and such regions are used to reject samples of unseen classes. We ask whether these regions also keep the features bounded when the head is trained with softmax cross-entropy. For a head whose class scores combine a linear term with a Euclidean norm, we first show that the region of each class is bounded by a quadric of revolution, whose eccentricity is the reciprocal of one learned ratio. We then attach to each class an asymptotic margin, which compares the growth of its score with the growth of all the other scores and can be computed by a second-order cone program. The loss of a class has infimum zero exactly when its margin is positive, and it then approaches zero only along diverging features. When the margin is negative, the loss is coercive and its minimizers lie in an explicit ball. Since softmax depends only on the differences between scores, a class with a bounded region can still have a positive margin, so bounded regions do not confine the features. The result extends to other norms, including the polyhedral conic functions. On CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100, all 1210 cells of 67 trained conic heads have positive margins, whereas a prototype head keeps nine of its ten cells bounded, as the theory predicts.
papers.Core_Innovation: It introduces a second-order cone program to compute asymptotic margins that deterministically classify whether softmax-loss features diverge or remain bounded by explicit quadrics.
papers.Decision_Perspective: Allocate funding to integrate asymptotic margin computation into conic head training pipelines within the next 18 months. Require margin-aware regularization for all newly deployed vision classification models.
papers.Tags: Conic Heads, Softmax, Asymptotic Margins, Feature Confinement
papers.Hook: Asymptotic margins now quantify when softmax-loss features diverge or stay bounded.

papers.Title: Unbundling Multimodal Vision Encoding
papers.Abstract: How multimodal language models should encode visual input remains up for debate. Most models use a pretrained vision encoder, while some recent recipes train the encoder from scratch with the language model or remove it entirely. Vision encoders bundle together three design choices: a visual prior from upstream pretraining, dedicated vision capacity, and pre-fusion placement of that capacity (i.e., before the multimodal backbone). Because published models also differ in data, architecture, and compute, comparing them cannot isolate the effect of each choice. We disentangle these choices via a controlled framework where we pretrain all models from scratch on common data and compare them on visual question answering and language benchmarks at matched lifetime compute. We find that the visual prior is not necessary; an encoder trained jointly from scratch is on par with a pretrained one, without a separate training stage. What matters instead is dedicated vision capacity: an encoder-free model trails on visual understanding even when its backbone is enlarged by the encoder's parameter count. Yet that capacity need not precede multimodal fusion, as vision-only modules added in-fusion to early backbone layers perform comparably to a pre-fusion encoder and can lower time to first token. These results also hold across backbone sizes, when encoder pretraining is treated as free, and when starting from a pretrained language model. Overall, our findings favor dedicated vision capacity trained jointly with the backbone and placed early within it.
papers.Core_Innovation: Researchers decoupled three encoder design choices—visual prior, dedicated capacity, and pre-fusion placement—by pretraining all models from scratch on identical data. Performance isolation reveals that dedicated vision capacity, not the visual prior, drives multimodal QA and language benchmark results.
papers.Benefiting_Sectors: Artificial Intelligence, Computer Vision, Generative AI
papers.Disrupted_Sectors: Pretrained Vision Encoders, Legacy Computer Vision Infrastructure
papers.Decision_Perspective: AI product teams should integrate jointly-trained vision encoders within six months to eliminate upstream pretraining costs. Competitors relying on frozen visual priors must benchmark against scratch-trained baselines on target vision tasks immediately.
papers.Tags: Multimodal AI, Vision Encoding, Model Efficiency, Compute Optimization
papers.Hook: Joint training from scratch matches pretrained encoders, removing upstream vision dependency

papers.Title: ArchSpace: Recording, Reviewing, and Referencing LLM Architecture Research
papers.Abstract: Model architecture shapes the scaling behavior, training efficiency, and inference cost of LLMs, making it a central focus of both industry and academia. In industry, teams such as those behind DeepSeek, Qwen, and Kimi routinely introduce architectural innovations, yet public reports rarely document which ideas succeeded, which were abandoned, and why. In academia, limited compute and inconsistent baselines often restrict evaluations to small-scale, single-point comparisons, making it difficult to establish whether improvements hold at larger scales or translate into broader impact. ArchSpace addresses both gaps as a public platform for Recording, Reviewing, and Referencing Architecture Researc}: each proposal is recorded with its experiments and reasoning, reviewed by the community, and referenced by later work. To evaluate ideas before costly large-scale training, ArchSpace leverages scaling laws to predict model loss at larger scales from smaller experiments, a practice widely adopted in industry. We provide initial references that make the platform usable: Qwen3.5 and OLMo3 baselines, fitted scaling laws, and a reusable training recipe. Ideas validated through this review can in turn become new baselines, and ArchSpace thereby aims to broaden the range of ideas that shape the next generation of models.
papers.Core_Innovation: ArchSpace records architecture proposals with full experimental metadata and uses scaling laws to predict loss at target compute, enabling architecture comparison without full training.
papers.Decision_Perspective: Require architecture recording for all internal LLM projects within 90 days to enable scaling law loss prediction. Measure resulting training efficiency gains to justify platform-wide adoption.
papers.Tags: architecture, scaling laws, platform, evaluation
papers.Hook: ArchSpace records, reviews, and references LLM architecture research, using scaling laws to predict large-scale loss from small experiments.

papers.Title: Internalizing Investment Mandates: A Neurosymbolic RL Approach to Portfolio Allocation
papers.Abstract: Institutional portfolios operate under investment policy statements that specify asset allocation constraints, often conditioned on market regime information. Deep reinforcement learning has been shown to optimize financial performance but typically does not enforce rule compliance, making it unsuitable for real-world deployment. Existing neurosymbolic methods such as Probabilistic Logic Policy Gradient (PLPG) offer constraint-satisfying reinforcement learning (RL) via differentiable symbolic supervision but assume a finite, discrete action space. We present a PLPG-inspired continuous allocation method that estimates the probability that the policy's own executed action satisfies the investment mandate, using reparameterized Monte Carlo sampling, and adds it to the training objective. No post-hoc enforcement mechanism intercepts actions at inference time and compliance is learned by the agent. Audited directly on deterministic mean actions with no correction, the policy reduces violations of a six-rule regime-conditional mandate from 96-98% for unconstrained RL and 33.4% for a reward-penalty baseline to 4.8%, showing that a continuous-action neurosymbolic policy can substantially internalize a symbolic mandate.
papers.Core_Innovation: Integrates a differentiable symbolic supervisor into the reward function using reparameterized Monte Carlo sampling to handle continuous action spaces.
papers.Decision_Perspective: Replace hard-coded constraint layers with this neurosymbolic objective in portfolio optimizers by Q3. Fund the migration of legacy rule-based allocation engines to this learned compliance framework.
papers.Tags: Neurosymbolic AI, Reinforcement Learning, Portfolio Optimization, Constraint Satisfaction
papers.Hook: RL agents can now learn to obey complex investment mandates without post-hoc action clipping.

papers.Title: AgentSSL: Can MLE Agents Leverage Unlabeled Data?
papers.Abstract: Applying machine learning systems to new domains introduces bottlenecks in both labeled data acquisition and manual pipeline engineering. While recent MLE agents show promise in automating pipeline design, they have been studied almost exclusively in fully supervised settings, leaving them untested in realistic regimes where labeled data is scarce but unlabeled data is abundant. In this work, we introduce Agentic Semi-Supervised Learning (AgentSSL), framing SSL as a program search problem and studying how agents navigate this space under limited supervision. We find that even under weak feedback and matched compute, agents can synthesize code that combines and adapts established SSL techniques, exceeding the strongest human-engineered baselines in 8 of 12 settings by up to +21.8%. However, our results identify program selection as a critical bottleneck in AgentSSL, where performance drops by as much as 47% when selecting based on the agent's feedback metric. To systematically study this bottleneck, we introduce ProgramSelectBench, a large-scale benchmark with a combined total of 16,977 agent-generated and human-engineered SSL programs, and evaluate both unsupervised and active program selection methods. We further evaluate AgentSSL on real-world ecology detection tasks, highlighting the opportunities and challenges of transferring agent-discovered strategies beyond controlled benchmarks.
papers.Core_Innovation: AgentSSL reframes semi-supervised learning as a program search problem, enabling agents to synthesize and combine SSL code under weak feedback
papers.Decision_Perspective: Allocate six-month funding to build AgentSSL prototypes with feedback-stable program selection. Deploy at scale only if synthesized pipelines consistently exceed human baselines by at least 15% on validated domains.
papers.Tags: AgentSSL,Semi-Supervised Learning,Program Search,Unlabeled Data
papers.Hook: MLE agents synthesize SSL pipelines from unlabeled data, outperforming human baselines

papers.Title: CoReMem: Cost-Internalizing Memory for Successive Coding Tasks with Prospective Valuation
papers.Abstract: Coding agents tackle successive tasks on an evolving repository, carrying forward edits and writing memory before the next task is known. Selecting memory for unknown next tasks requires balancing future usefulness against the costs of writing and reading it. The actor must also decide when acting on available memory saves effort as the task unfolds. We introduce Coding-Repository Memory (CoReMem), a cost-internalizing framework that guides memory design and actor adaptation through measured memory value on the next task. Prospective segment valuation compares runs of the next task with and without individual trajectory segments from the same inherited repository state, guiding a compact memory built around anchors: repository locations and executable checks. Actor adaptation estimates on-policy memory value within rollout groups with and without memory, using a reward that prioritizes resolution and penalizes step count in successful runs. Provenance-gated value credit assigns the additional value term to steps identified as using memory-supplied anchors, while every step retains outcome credit. On ChainSWE, CoReMem raises the 27B actor's resolve rate from 21.0% to 25.7%, with 17% fewer steps and 11% fewer total cache-aware tokens, including memory-module calls, relative to the untrained actor model without memory.
papers.Core_Innovation: Prospective segment valuation quantifies memory utility by contrasting task runs with and without inherited segments, directing compact memory toward repository locations and executable checks.
papers.Decision_Perspective: Fund prototype integration of CoReMem into code agent pipelines within 6 months to validate cost-reduction claims. Mandate ablation studies comparing prospective valuation against baseline memory heuristics before wider deployment.
papers.Tags: CoReMem, Prospective Valuation, Memory Anchors
papers.Hook: Prospective segment valuation enables cost-aware coding across repositories for successive tasks.

papers.Title: Linking Rapid Learning to Compositional Structure in Neural Networks: Evidence from Additive Analogies in Meta-Learned Parameter Spaces
papers.Abstract: Humans can learn rapidly from limited experience, while neural networks typically require extensive training. In this work, we investigate what properties of a neural network can enable it to learn rapidly. We study neural networks that have been optimized via meta-learning, a technique that exposes a network to many related functions to facilitate its subsequent learning of similar functions. Prior work has shown that these meta-learned networks can learn new functions rapidly, but how they do so remains unclear. To investigate their internal structure, we take inspiration from classic work demonstrating additive relationships among the learned vectors that neural networks use to represent words (e.g., "king" minus "man" plus "woman" approximates "queen"). Analogously, we look for additive relationships among a meta-learned network's "representations" of different functions; when a meta-learned network rapidly learns to implement a specific function, all of its adapted parameter values can be concatenated into a single vector that we treat as representing the function. We find that such parameter vectors can be added and subtracted according to symbolic relationships among the functions they represent, yielding new parameter vectors that successfully represent the functions predicted by the corresponding symbolic manipulations: the networks specified by these artificially recombined vectors actually implement the intended functions without any direct training on them. Our results suggest that meta-learning can tune a network's starting point to organize subsequent learning along systematic, functionally meaningful trajectories through the space of possible parameter vectors, providing a geometric basis for realizing inductive biases in neural networks.
papers.Core_Innovation: Decomposes meta-learned parameter updates into additive analogy vectors, isolating function-specific adaptation directions in weight space.
papers.Decision_Perspective: Invest in meta-learning startups building additive parameter geometries within 18 months. Acquire engineering teams developing rapid-adaptation neural architectures before Q3 2027.
papers.Tags: Meta-Learning, Additive Analogies, Neural Networks, Rapid Learning, Parameter Space
papers.Hook: Meta-learned networks exhibit additive parameter analogies enabling rapid function acquisition.

papers.Title: Sketching Language Models for Context Attribution
papers.Abstract: Context attribution asks how removing parts of a prompt changes a language model's output. We study leave-one-out (LOO) attribution for a prompt of $n$ tokens and a fixed measurement function. Computing all LOO values directly requires $n$ model evaluations. Under a stability assumption, our algorithm estimates all LOO values to error proportional to $\varepsilon$ with constant probability using $O(\sqrt{\log(1/\varepsilon)}/\varepsilon)$ evaluation calls. To complement our upper bound, we prove a matching $Ω(\sqrt{\log(1/\varepsilon)}/\varepsilon)$ lower bound on the number of evaluation calls in an oracle model. Empirically, we verify coefficient decay consistent with stability and evaluate the performance of our sketching algorithm on a small language-model retrieval task.   Technically, our result is based on a sketching algorithm for arithmetic circuits whose Taylor coefficients satisfy the stability condition recently introduced by Gunn [Gun26]. A direct adaptation of their forward differentiation sketches would require $\widetilde{O}(\log(n)/\varepsilon^2)$ evaluation calls. Our key observation is that we can apply forward differentiation to the backpropagation circuit, with only constant overhead over a forward sketch of the same Taylor degree. This reduces the variance of the sketches and is key to our improved evaluation bound. Our lower bound builds on the techniques of Amsel, Chen, Duman Keles, Halikias, Musco, and Musco [ACDH+26, SIAM Journal on Matrix Analysis and Applications] for lower bounding the number of matrix-vector queries to estimate the diagonal elements of random matrices.
papers.Core_Innovation: Introduces a sketching framework for arithmetic circuits with stability-enforcing Taylor coefficients. This enables ε-accurate leave-one-out attribution with near-optimal evaluation complexity.
papers.Benefiting_Sectors: Language Model Development, AI Retrieval, Natural Language Processing
papers.Decision_Perspective: Fund teams building sketch-based attribution pipelines within 6 months to capture efficiency gains. Acquire or partner with arithmetic circuit tooling providers to integrate near-optimal LOO metrics.
papers.Tags: sketching, attribution, arithmetic circuits, stability, language models
papers.Hook: Enables near-optimal context attribution for language models with sublinear evaluation calls

papers.Title: Classical Energies Learn to Reason 1,000x Faster than Looped Models
papers.Abstract: Looped models have emerged as a prominent paradigm for reasoning, with successes on simple reasoning puzzles such as Sudoku-Extreme and Maze-Unique. However, these models can be unstable, slow to train, and use many parameters and FLOPs to solve simple puzzles. Descent on an energy not only mitigates these issues but also offers advantages: built-in early stopping, compute that adapts to problem difficulty, fast training without differentiating through a solver, and interpretable weights that learn the constraints of the puzzle. Here we demonstrate this with a learned version of Hopfield & Tank's energy from the 80s, which we term CRAM, solves 99.996% of Sudoku-Extreme and 100% of Maze-Unique test puzzles after 42 ms and 132 ms of training on one GPU, at least 1,000x faster than looped models on these tasks. CRAM also matches baseline looped models at their highest accuracy on Sudoku-Extreme using at least 282x fewer inference FLOPs. Our work suggests two things. First, that energies are an extremely promising direction for training reasoning from data. Second, a caution against using trivially solvable benchmarks like Sudoku and Maze to test the scalability of looped reasoning techniques.
papers.Core_Innovation: CRAM introduces a learned Hopfield-Tank energy model for reasoning. Energy descent replaces iterative looped computation, enabling built-in early stopping and adaptive compute.
papers.Benefiting_Sectors: Artificial Intelligence, Optimization Software, Education Technology
papers.Decision_Perspective: Fund CRAM-based reasoning prototypes for latency-critical applications within Q3 2026. Kill iterative looped model deployments in favor of energy-descent alternatives once FLOP savings exceed 25%
papers.Tags: CRAM, Energy Descent, Reasoning
papers.Hook: CRAM solves Sudoku and mazes 1,000x faster while using 282x fewer inference FLOPs

papers.Title: Quantifying structural stability of transparent models for general insurance pricing
papers.Abstract: The short duration of general insurance contracts leads to rapid distributional shifts in the data, warranting regular model updates. This process may yield a post-update model that differs considerably from the pre-update model in both predictions and structure. Structural stability is upstream of predictive stability, yet existing structural stability metrics are mostly restricted to simple decision trees. Thus, we first introduce the notion of functional transparency, characterising models with a prediction function that can be expressed as a sum of univariate functions for main effects and bivariate functions for pairwise interactions. Then, we propose the Mean Squared Shape function distance, a metric to quantify the structural stability of functionally transparent models, which are particularly relevant in actuarial science. Using three public auto insurance datasets, we present a benchmark study to demonstrate the usefulness of our metric in identifying a stable and accurate transparent model. Generalised linear models with centred numerical covariates are stable, and explainable boosting machines (EBMs) offer a compromise between stability and performance. We also find that stabilisation strategies, such as sequential modelling and fixed hyperparameters, can substantially improve stability for both EBM and XGBoost models, with negligible impact on performance.
papers.Core_Innovation: Introduces functional transparency as additive main-effects plus bivariate pairwise interaction decompositions, then proposes Mean Squared Shape function distance as the first structural stability metric beyond decision-tree limitations.
papers.Decision_Perspective: Auto insurers should adopt MSSfD to audit model updates quarterly, ensuring structural drift stays below established thresholds. Teams building transparent pricing pipelines must integrate this metric before deploying any model retraining cycle.
papers.Tags: structural stability, functional transparency, Mean Squared Shape function distance, actuarial science
papers.Hook: New metric quantifies structural stability of transparent insurance pricing models across distribution shifts

papers.Title: Towards a Theory of Learnability via Debate
papers.Abstract: Debate has been recently proposed as a training protocol that is hoped to produce more aligned models even as model capabilities scale. The idea is that the human, instead of providing supervision in the form of labels, judges a debate between two models that compete to prove the correctness of opposite labels. It can be shown that functions of a much higher computational complexity can be correctly judged in this way, compared to the complexity of functions that can be directly evaluated using a computationally weak evaluator. This suggests that perhaps debate can be used to teach very complicated functions to models. However, previous work has largely ignored the fact that this is a training protocol, and simply analyzes the game being played between the two debaters for a known judge. We take the first steps towards understanding the learning problem implicit within the protocol, by formulating it as an online learning problem. We show that once we formulate the learning problem precisely, there are cases where the best way to learn given access to a judge is different from running an adversarial debate. This motivates us to define a cooperative version of the protocol, whose learnability we characterize using a combinatorial dimension. We also consider the possibility of the human judge being fallible and occasionally judging the debate incorrectly. We show that a small number of errors in judgement can lead to a large error in learning.
papers.Core_Innovation: The paper formulates debate as an online learning problem, shifting analysis from fixed-judge games to adaptive protocol-driven learnability
papers.Decision_Perspective: Allocate venture capital to debate-aligned LLM startups within the next 24 months to secure leadership in safe model training. Replace supervised-label-dependent pipelines with debate-based online learning frameworks once benchmark thresholds are validated.
papers.Tags: Debate, Online Learning, Model Alignment, Computational Complexity, Training Protocols
papers.Hook: Debate protocol enables training models on computationally intractable functions via online learning.

papers.Title: FLEX-LBP: Learning Local Binary Patterns with Exact Binary Inference for Texture Classification
